loc.section: In practice there are two broad ways that allowances are allocated: providing them for free or selling them through auctions. When distributing allowances, policymakers will seek to achieve some or all of the following objectives (which are not always mutually compatible): ^S Preserving incentives for cost-effective abatement. In attempting to achieve any or all of the objectives, policymakers must ensure that an integral objective of the ETS is maintained: ensuring covered firms are incentivized to abate emissions in a cost-effective manner and as far as possible through the value chain. ^S Managing the transition to an ETS. There are numerous issues involved in transitioning to an ETS that a policymaker may wish to manage through the approach to allowance allocation. Some relate to the distribution of costs and value, including possible loss of asset value (“stranded assets”), undesirable impacts on consumers and communities, and a desire to recognize those who have taken early reduction actions. Additionally, the potential to create windfall profits where firms pass on carbon costs to consumers despite receiving free allowances is higher under some methods of allocation, and policymakers can seek to minimize this risk. Other issues relate to risks such as participants initially having a low capacity to trade or resistance to participation among some companies where institutional capability is weak. ^S Reducing the risk of carbon leakage or loss of competitiveness. Carbon leakage occurs when production moves from a jurisdiction with a carbon price to another jurisdiction without a carbon price or with a lower carbon price. This can occur in the near term through domestic firms losing market share to international competitors, and over the longer term through firms’ decisions as to where to invest in plants and equipment. These risks present a combination of undesirable environmental, economic, and political outcomes for policymakers. Avoiding these factors is always one of the most controversial and important aspects when considering the design of an ETS, and allocation in particular. There is little empirical evidence of carbon leakage to date, with most ETSs having taken steps to reduce carbon leakage risks. This is likely in part due to low carbon prices thus far, but a wide range of other factors also affect investment and production decisions, and are also likely to have played a role in limiting carbon leakage. ^S Raising revenue. The allowances created when an ETS is established are valuable. By selling allowances, often through auctioning, ETSs can generate significant amounts of public revenue that can then be used for other purposes. ^S Supporting price discovery in markets. The economic efficiency of an ETS results from price discovery by trading allowances. Generally, this occurs in liquid secondary markets; however, in smaller markets with lower liquidity, allocation by auctions can play an important role in price discovery by matching supply and demand in the market and providing transparent information on market conditions. The distribution of allowances will be a contentious issue, and finding a solution that is acceptable to government, stakeholders, and the general public is critical to getting started. loc.section: National greenhouse-gas accounting should reflect how countries’ policies and behaviours affect global emissions. Actions that contribute to reduced global emissions should be credited, and actions that increase them should be penal- ized. This is essential if accounting is to serve as accurate guidance for climate policy. Yet this principle is not satisfied by the two most common accounting methods. Production-based accounting used under the Kyoto Protocol does not account for carbon leakage—the phenomenon of countries reducing their domestic emissions by shifting carbon-intensive production abroad^1 . Consumption-based accounting^2,3 (also called carbon footprinting) does not credit countries for cleaning up their export industries, and it also punishes some types of trade that could contribute to more carbon efficient production worldwide. We propose an improvement to consumption-based carbon accounting that takes technology differences in export sectors into account and thereby tends to more correctly reflect how national policy changes affect total global emissions. We also present empirical results showing how this new measure redraws the global emissions map.

Carbon quantity per unit of fuel or material, expressed per energy unit or per mass unit depending on the source.
Tradable unit for one tonne CO2e of reduction or removal, defined with different boundaries for organizations (value chain) and cities (accounting boundary).
Definitions of a tradable instrument representing one tCO2e of reduction or removal, framed with differing accounting boundaries (organization vs community).
Alternative ways of assigning emission responsibility (production, consumption, income-based, benchmark-value) that give different regional results.
Tonnes of carbon per tonne dry matter used to convert biomass and dead organic matter to carbon, with pool-, chapter- and edition-specific defaults.

Relocation of production or emissions to jurisdictions with weaker climate constraints, defined differently as a policy concern, a country-accounting artefact, or an outcome requiring a global emissions increase.
Variant definitions of carbon leakage as relocation of production or emissions to regions with weaker climate policy, from accounting and ETS-policy perspectives.
CO2 estimated from carbon entering minus carbon leaving in products and by-products, multiplied by 44/12, as applied to coke production and petrochemicals.

n: Carbon pool definitions across IPCC AFOLU guidance
s: The set of AFOLU carbon pools (five pools, with HWP added in the 2019 Refinement) as defined in successive IPCC guidance.

n: Carbon pool stock change estimation approach
s: Generic ways to estimate annual carbon stock change in a pool, either from annual gains and losses or from stock differences between two times.
Alternative ways of attributing emissions to actors, e.g. production-based, consumption-based, and upstream/downstream-sharing measures.
Alternative rules for allocating emissions to regions or entities: production-based, consumption-based, income-based, value-added-based, product benchmark and TBC shared responsibility.
Alternative principles for allocating carbon emission responsibility, such as production-based, consumption-based and technology-adjusted consumption-based accounting.
Different principles for assigning emissions to a responsible party, such as the producing territory or the consuming city or individual.
Alternative ways of assigning total emissions to producers or final consumers, here the full producer and full consumer extremes.
Alternative ways of assigning emission responsibility, such as production, consumption, income-based and shared producer/consumer responsibility.

Alternative principles for assigning emissions responsibility between producers, consumers and other actors, including welfare-share, individual consumption elasticity and shared-responsibility approaches.
Ways of assigning emissions to regions or sectors using multi-regional input-output models: consumption-based (Leontief), income-based (Ghosh) and modular reformulations.
Two ways to estimate emissions from processing sold intermediate products: activity-based site-specific, or mass times industry-average factor.
Alternative data-tier methods (fuel-, distance-, spend-based) for estimating upstream transportation emissions under Scope 3 Category 4.
Alternative methods (supplier-specific, waste-type-specific, average treatment) for estimating Scope 3 Category 5 waste emissions.
IPCC category-specific QC checklist (Annex 6A.1 A2) as published in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Estimation of an emission category's variance from its total and uncertainty, with different formulas for symmetric and asymmetric uncertainty.
Alternative ways to attribute captured CO2 and its capture and transport emissions between CO2 producer and user in a product carbon footprint.
The UN product classification, present in two versions (2.1 and 3) in different sources.

n: CH4 emission factors for FeSi and Si alloy
s: Default (Tier 1) and operation-specific (Tier 2) CH4 emission factors for ferrosilicon and silicon metal production.
Annual CH4 emissions from livestock manure systems, formulated differently in the 2006 Guidelines (EF x head count) and the 2019 Refinement (N x VS x AWMS x EF).

n: CH4 emissions from SWDS net of recovery and oxidation
s: Annual CH4 from solid waste disposal as generated CH4 less recovered CH4, reduced by the oxidation factor, in 2006 and 2019 versions that place R_T differently.

n: Changes in net worth due to saving and capital transfers (B101)
s: SNA 2025 item B101, whose objects disagree on whether it is an analytical aggregate or a balancing item.
Provincial or inter-regional input-output table sets for China that differ in years, region and sector detail and source, and are not interchangeable without a concordance.

n: Choice between product-by-product and industry-by-industry IOT
s: Selecting a table type for analysis depends on purpose, with differing source preferences.
Treatments for attributing combined heat and power emissions to electricity and heat outputs and to reporting scopes.
Different framings of circular economy as a contested concept (IPCC) versus a concrete strategy set (GRO24).
The two complementary GPC ways of reporting city emissions: by scope (where emissions occur) and by city-induced activities (BASIC/BASIC+).
Clinker CO2 emission factors in IPCC 2006 cement methods that differ in whether they are corrected for cement kiln dust (CKD).
Tier-dependent clinker CO2 emission factors that differ in whether they are corrected for cement kiln dust (CKD).
Recycling allocation approach in the GHG Protocol Product Standard, described with different conditions and section references across sources.
A secondary product of a process or life cycle that has value and is a candidate for allocation, defined differently in the Scope 3 and Product Standards.
Definitions of a co-product used in the GHG Protocol standards, which differ in wording and emphasis.

n: CO2 capture deduction from reported emissions
s: Rules on whether and how captured CO2 is subtracted from reported emissions, with differing scopes and conditions across IPCC 2006 and 2019 materials.

n: CO2 completeness check for non-energy fuel use
s: Check that reported process or non-energy-use CO2 is complete relative to the carbon supplied as non-energy fuel, in 2006 and 2019 versions.
Ways of combining multiple greenhouse gases into one reported quantity, with GWP100 weighting or without any weighting.
Tier 1 production-data and Tier 3 mass-balance estimates of CO2 from alumina sintering.

n: CO2 from other process uses of carbonates
s: Tier 2 and Tier 3 ways of estimating CO2 from other process uses of carbonates.
Tier 1 and Tier 2 IPCC 2006 estimates of CO2 from paraffin wax use.

n: CO2 inputs from oxidation of non-CO2 carbon gases
s: Conversion of CH4, CO and NMVOC emissions into the CO2 eventually formed in the atmosphere, with differing parameters across IPCC versions.
Rules for converting non-CO2 gases to CO2-equivalent using GWP values, with differing requirements about source and time horizon across IPCC editions.
Ratio of standard deviation to mean used as a relative dispersion measure, applied over different samples (MRIO realizations or accounting perspectives).

The ratio of standard deviation to mean used as a relative dispersion measure, applied differently across IPCC statistics, MRIO uncertainty of CBCA and the sensitivity of provincial CEs to accounting principle.
CO2 from metallurgical coke production by carbon balance, from simplified Tier 1b to Tier 2 with country-specific carbon contents.
Different framings of CHP: general glossary definition, inventory reporting category 1A1a ii, and purchaser-side allocation under GHG Protocol Scope 2.

Simultaneous generation of electricity and useful heat, with variants adding cooling (CCHP) or defined as a reporting category (1A1a ii). Key to responsibility allocation between electricity and heat outputs.
Versions of the dimensionless combustion factor (proportion of fuel actually combusted) in the IPCC 2006 and 2019 guidance.
The requirement that an inventory cover all sources and activities within its defined boundary, with disclosed exclusions, defined differently for national, corporate, product and city boundaries.
Activity-weighted average emission factor across sub-applications, defined in the IPCC 2006 and 2019 ODS-substitutes chapters.
A range or interval estimate that may enclose the true value of an unknown quantity at a stated confidence level, typically 95 percent, with different wording in IPCC 2006 and 2019.

n: Confidence interval definitions across IPCC inventory guidance
s: The 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement define a confidence interval with different wording, one for a fixed unknown quantity and one for a population parameter.
Conventions for protecting confidential data in inventories, ETS reporting and official statistics, typically by aggregation, anonymisation or restricted access.

n: Confidential data handling in inventories and reporting
s: Rules for protecting confidential source data in inventories and corporate reporting. They use aggregation, avoidance, transparent QA/QC or auditor-only access.

n: Confidential data notation in IPPU background tables
s: IPCC reporting convention for confidential entries in IPPU background tables: notation key C or aggregate figures, plus a documentation-box note.
Accounting principle that methods and data stay consistent over time with changes documented, stated separately in IPCC 2006 and GHG Protocol Scope 3.
Term used for aggregating accounts: eliminating intra-sector flows in SNA versus combining company GHG data in the GHG Protocol.
Operations that aggregate unit-level data into a group or sector account. They differ between the GHG Protocol (combine emissions) and the SNA (eliminate intra-sector flows).
Allocation of production emissions to final consumers via input-output (MRIO) models, with differing formulations of imports, exports and household direct emissions.
Allocation of emissions to final consumers using multi-region input-output models, in formulations that add embodied imports and subtract embodied exports or use the Leontief inverse on final demand.

Allocation of emissions or other impacts along the supply chain to the entity or region of final consumption, with differing boundaries, gas bases and treatment of imports, exports, aviation and shipping.

Family of definitions that attribute emissions along the supply chain to final consumption, differing in spatial scale (city, province, nation), trade treatment, gas and sector coverage, and formulation (Leontief-type, network-flow, MRIO footprint). The catalog contains no formula.
Family of approaches that assign emissions from production and supply chains to final consumers or final demand, differing in boundary, formula and treatment of shared responsibility.
Approaches that allocate emissions to final consumers or intermediate users through input-output or embodied-emission calculations, covering full and partial transfer of upstream emissions.

Different tests for whether an entity falls inside an accounting boundary through control: SNA/BPM7 corporate-policy control (more than 50 percent voting) versus GHG Protocol operational and financial control.
Different rules for deciding whether an entity is controlled and therefore consolidated, used in GHG Protocol organisational boundaries and in SNA corporate classification.

The criterion that decides which entities are included in an accounting boundary, defined differently in national accounts (corporate-policy control, >50% voting) and in the GHG Protocol (operational or financial control).
A partial life-cycle boundary used in different standards, with different end points and different treatment of the reporting company's own sources.

Different standards define a cradle-to-gate boundary differently regarding whose own-company emissions are included and where the gate sits (receipt by the buyer, producer's point of sale, or the company's exit gate).

n: Crop residue N input F_CR (IPCC version-specific)
s: Annual N in crop residues returned to soils, defined with different default tables in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: Crop residue N input F_CR (version series)
s: The annual N in crop residues returned to soils, in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement versions.
IPCC Cropland land-use category as defined, reported and used in different volumes and versions of the 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement.

n: Cropland SOC relative stock change factors
s: Tier 1 default F_LU, F_MG and F_I factors for mineral cropland soils in the 2006 and 2019 editions.
Rules that prevent the same emissions from being counted in two sectors, categories or downstream uses.

n: Cross-entropy balancing of regional supply-demand distributions
s: Minimum cross-entropy (KL divergence) estimation of an adjusted regional supply and demand distribution relative to a prior, used to construct provincial input-output tables.

n: Cultivated organic soil carbon loss (A × EF)
s: Annual carbon loss from cultivated organic soils is computed as area times a climate-specific emission factor, with worksheets per land-conversion category.
Regional default dairy cattle input data for Tier 1 emission factors, in 2006 and 2019 editions.
Documentation of data sources, assumptions, procedures and quality controls for a GHG inventory, as required by the GHG Protocol standards.
Schemes that score data quality for LCA or PCF data using different indicators, scales and aggregation.
Sets of indicators used to assess the representativeness and reliability of data in GHG inventories and product footprints.
Frameworks for rating the representativeness and quality of activity or emission-factor data. They differ in indicator set and scoring scale.

n: Data quality indicators for GHG accounting
s: Sets of indicators used to judge the representativeness and quality of activity and emission-factor data, which differ in number and scoring across standards.

n: Dead organic matter change on land conversion (Equation 2.23)
s: Variants of the dead wood and litter carbon change calculation on converted land, differing in sign convention and time treatment.

n: Dead wood and litter carbon stock change method
s: Alternative gain-loss and stock-difference equations for annual change in dead wood or litter carbon, in the 2006 and 2019 editions.
Definitions of the dead wood pool that differ in the lower diameter bound applied to dead roots.
Definitions of the dead wood pool that use different diameter thresholds and inclusions for roots and wood.
Indicators relating economic activity (GDP or other aggregates) to emissions or physical flows, defined differently across sources.
A relationship in which an environmental pressure grows more slowly than an economic or well-being driver.
Default EF4, EF5, FracGASF, FracGASM and FracLEACH values for indirect soil N2O, with edition-specific values.

n: Default N loss fractions from manure management (Tables 10.22/10.23)
s: Default fractions of excreted N lost from manure management, as gas loss, leaching or total loss, differently split across the 2006 and 2019 editions.
Default fraction of feed N intake retained by livestock, in 2006 and 2019 editions.
Default livestock N excretion rates by category and region, in 2006 and 2019 editions.
Rules across guidelines and standards on when default emission factors or parameters may be used instead of site-, plant- or country-specific data, with differing conditions and restrictions.

n: Deferral of organic soil methods to 2013 Wetlands Supplement
s: The 2019 Refinement chapters give no refinement for drained organic soils and refer to the 2013 Wetlands Supplement.
Loss of forest cover, defined by SEEA CF as complete loss of tree cover with a change of use and by IPCC 2006 as direct human-induced conversion to non-forest.
Degradable organic carbon content of waste that drives CH4 emissions, expressed as a fraction, a mass (DOCm) or tonnes C per tonne waste depending on source and version.
Physical depletion is computed differently for non-renewable, timber and aquatic resources.
Decrease in a natural resource stock from extraction exceeding regeneration or growth, defined physically in SEEA-CF and in physical and monetary terms (P8/NF35) in the 2025 SNA.
Two SNA formulations of depreciation: decline in asset value, and decrease in present value of future capital services.
Fraction of contaminants or input gases destroyed or removed by an emission control device, used in IPCC guidelines with differing symbols and contexts.

Direct emissions are defined differently across sources: by company ownership/control (GHG Protocol), by the sector where they arise (IPCC AR6), or as process-level data determined by monitoring or mass balance (product standards).
Direct emissions defined differently depending on whether the boundary is organisational control, process/product measurement, sector territory or producer responsibility.
The term direct emissions is used with different boundaries: organisational control, process measurement data, sector-of-origin assignment, and sector direct pressure in MRIO.

n: Direct N2O emissions from managed soils
s: Estimation of direct N2O from managed soils via tiered IPCC equations and the community-scale protocol adaptation, which differ in disaggregation and units.

n: Direct N2O emissions from manure management
s: Calculation of direct N2O from manure management systems from N excretion, MMS fractions and EF3, as an aggregate equation, a per-MMS step and a worksheet.
Tiered equations for annual direct N2O-N emissions from managed soils, from N inputs, organic soils and urine/dung deposition.

n: Direct purchases abroad by residents (treatment in tables)
s: The same economic item is placed differently across table frameworks: an adjustment row in SUTs (national versus domestic concept) and a separate column in the SNA multi-country IO table.
Standards and guidelines (GHG Protocol, IPCC, GPC, Chinese MRV guidelines) with differing boundaries and purposes for emissions inventory and reporting.

n: Disclosure-standard boundary treatments of GHG removals
s: Different standards treat removals differently: excluded from Scope 3, included in the product inventory, excluded from GRI gross targets.
A difference between reported or estimated inventory values and a reference, where the reference is either properly applied standards (GHG Protocol) or independent datasets (IPCC QA/QC).
The SNA disposable-income balancing item in its gross (B6g) and net (B6n) forms.
Scope 3 calculations that multiply activity distance (and mass, volume or passengers) by a mode- or vehicle-specific emission factor, adapted per category.
Fraction of degradable organic carbon that decomposes in a solid waste disposal site, defined differently in IPCC 2006 (single default) and IPCC 2019 (varies by waste type).

n: DOM carbon stock change estimation approaches
s: Alternative gain-loss and stock-difference ways of estimating annual carbon stock change in dead wood and litter, in the 2006 GL and the 2019 Refinement.
The GRO24 resource-extraction indicator and its several differently-worded extractions.
Estimating CH4 from domestic wastewater via emission factors per pathway, with different factor definitions in IPCC 2006, IPCC 2019 and the community-scale protocol.
Default uncertainty ranges for domestic wastewater CH4 emission factor and activity parameters, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
Default methane correction factors for domestic wastewater treatment and discharge pathways, in 2006 and 2019 editions.
Different standards define double counting as multiple parties or scopes claiming the same emissions, reductions or units, with differing scope and tolerance.

Rules in the disclosure standards and IPCC inventory guidance that prevent the same emissions from being counted twice at different boundaries (organisation, scope, product category, national inventory).

n: Double counting (duplicate claims of emissions or reductions)
s: Several parties, scopes, targets or units claim the same emissions or reductions; the standards define it differently and differ in whether it is avoidable or inherent.
Different standards define double counting differently: overlap of claims between entities, across scopes, across targets, or in credits and reductions.
Emissions occurring after the reporting company's own boundary in the product or value chain.
Responsibility is allocated to the downstream or income side, i.e. to those who receive payments from primary inputs, rather than to final consumers.
Approaches that allocate emissions or environmental pressure back to primary inputs or income, as opposed to producer or consumer allocation.
Rules for how much of a sector's embodied indirect emissions are passed to downstream users versus retained as producer responsibility.

The word 'downstream' is used for emissions or responsibility located after a reference actor in the supply chain, with different boundaries in GHG Protocol standards, input-output responsibility literature and ETS regulation.
Tier 2 non-energy CO2 from direct reduced iron computed from fuel energy times carbon content times 44/12, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
Allocation of a common process's emissions among outputs in proportion to their market or economic value, with differing boundary and formula presentations across sources.
Rule that upstream or downstream environmental pressure attached to an economic flow is proportional to the monetary value of that flow via sector intensities.

The property that environmental pressure attached to an inter-sectoral economic flow is proportional to the monetary size of that flow via a sector intensity, stated in upstream-only and upstream-plus-downstream forms.
Allocation of emissions from a multi-output process or facility to outputs in proportion to their market or economic value, in different corporate and product-level standards.

Variant definitions of the geographic boundary of an economy, from the single-government SEEA-CF definition to the broader SNA 2025 wording that includes any statistical area and currency or economic unions.
Methods that allocate emissions via input-output models, either as sector or revenue factors for supply chains or as regional MRIO consumption-based totals.
Methods that use environmentally extended input-output models to allocate emissions to final demand or to products, either as Leontief-based consumption emissions or as emissions per unit revenue.
Default emission factor for N2O from urine and dung N deposited by grazing animals, with different values in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Tier-by-tier lists of supporting information needed for transparent reporting of electronics manufacturing emission estimates, in 2006 and 2019 editions.
Tier 1 default emission factors for fluorinated gases from electronics manufacturing under 2006 numbering (Table 6.2) and 2019 numbering (Table 6.6).
Activity data basis for electronics industry Tier 2 (and 3) methods: gas purchases in 2006 versus gas consumption with heel correction in 2019.
Methods for distributing the emissions of a multi-output activity across products, here via physical relationships such as mass, volume or energy.
Accounting boundary that assigns emissions or physical flows either to the residence of the emitting unit or to the territory where the emission occurs.
Different principles (residence, ownership, source country, consuming country) for deciding which party or economy is assigned an emission.
Boundary and allocation rules from disclosure standards (GHG Protocol Scope 2 and Scope 3) that define what emissions an organization reports and how they are quantified.
Average uptime of emission control systems, defined as 1 minus total down-time over total run-time, aggregated by process type or by facility.
A coefficient converting an activity quantity into emissions, with units and boundaries that vary by source and sector.

n: Emission factor approach (emission factor × activity quantity)
s: Emissions are estimated as an emission factor times an activity quantity, where the activity quantity may be generic activity data, equipment nameplate capacity or a chemical bank.

n: Emission factor (coefficient per unit activity, unit-specific forms)
s: Emission factors share the generic meaning of emissions per unit of activity but are expressed on different activity and unit bases (kg/TJ, m3/t coal, g/kg dry matter, kg CO2/kWh).

n: Emission factor (coefficient per unit of activity)
s: A coefficient converting an activity quantity into GHG emissions or removals, whose unit and activity basis (kg/TJ, m3/t, g/kg dry matter, kgCO2/kWh, ha-yr) vary by source and sector.

n: Emission intensity / emission coefficient (per unit of output)
s: Emissions per unit of output, defined on different bases: dollar of sector output, euro of industry output or physical product unit.

n: Emission intensity (emissions per unit of activity or output)
s: Emissions divided by some denominator (monetary output, physical product, functional unit or activity data); the denominators differ, so the values are not interchangeable.
Alternative schemes for grouping greenhouse gas emissions into sectors: the IPCC 2006 and 2019 five-sector national schemes and the GPC six-sector city scheme.
Average uptime of emission control systems as one minus total downtime over total runtime, defined per process type (Eq 6.20) or per facility (Eq 6.27).

The term 'emissions' is defined differently by IPCC/UNFCCC (territorial GHG release to the atmosphere), SEEA/SNA (releases by economic units), GHG Protocol and sector guidance (CO2e shorthand), so the boundary depends on the framework.

n: Emissions embodied in trade and consumption-based attribution
s: Different definitions of emissions attributed along supply chains or trade to final consumers, differing in scope, full versus partial transfer and unit basis.
Emissions per unit of some activity measure, where the chosen denominator (primary energy, value added, revenue) and emissions boundary change the meaning.
Emissions divided by an output measure, where the denominator may be monetary output, physical product units or lifetime functional units, so values are not interchangeable.
Alternative reference bases for expressing a percentage emissions reduction goal: base-year absolute, base-year intensity, or business-as-usual scenario.
The shared definition of gaseous and particulate releases to the atmosphere by establishments and households, used in SEEA and the supply-use handbook.
A market mechanism that caps total emissions and requires or issues tradable permits or allowances per unit of emissions.
Different frameworks (SNA, GRI, GHG Protocol Scope 3) define which persons count as employees for different purposes.
The term 'employee' is defined differently in SNA (remuneration agreement), GRI (reporting categories) and GHG Protocol Scope 3 Category 7 (commuting scope).
Contractual instruments that convey attributes of generated energy separately from the physical energy, used for market-based Scope 2 claims.
Emission-factor times livestock-number equations for enteric CH4 with different output units and aggregation levels.
Activity-data × emission-factor estimates of methane from livestock enteric fermentation, with different unit scalings in community and IPCC sources.

n: Enteric fermentation CH4 estimation by livestock category
s: Methods in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement for estimating enteric CH4 from livestock by multiplying emission factors by animal numbers, at Tier 1 and Tier 2.
Percentage of gross energy intake converted to methane in livestock Tier 2 methods, a different quantity from the manure and waste MCFs.
Variant statements of the SNA 2025 entrepreneurial income measure, as a balancing item or as corporate income including property income.
Indicators that allocate environmental pressure or emissions between producers, consumers and other agents, with differing allocation rules.
Methods that attach environmental pressures to input-output tables, either single-region EEIO models for product footprints or multi-regional EE MRIO tables.
Alternative Tier 3 ways to estimate equipment leak emissions from screening data: screening ranges versus unit-specific correlation.

n: Equipment leak emission estimation from screening values
s: Correlation-based IPCC 2019 approaches that convert screening values of leaking equipment into fluorinated GHG emission rates.

The statistical unit used to split production by location and activity for supply-use and input-output compilation, defined with differing strictness about secondary activities and single-product scope.

The statistical production unit used in national accounts and supply-use/input-output compilation. Sources vary between a single-location principal-activity unit, a single-product unit, and a unit allowed secondary activities.

Arrangements in which an emissions trading system recognizes allowances from another system for compliance, defined either broadly (with or without restrictions) or narrowly (full mutual recognition).

n: Excluded carbon (non-energy use carbon excluded from fuel combustion)
s: Carbon in feedstocks, reductants and non-energy products that is excluded from fuel combustion emissions, as defined in the IPCC 2006 and 2019 glossaries and the Reference Approach chapter.

n: Exclusion/cut-off threshold rules for product carbon footprints
s: Rules that allow or require exclusion of minor processes or products from a carbon footprint boundary, with differing thresholds and versions.
Different ways of deriving N2O emission factors from field measurements of N2O fluxes and N inputs or deposition.
Carbon accounting that attributes fossil-fuel emissions to the country or point of fuel extraction rather than combustion or consumption, with several slightly different definitions across sources.
Attribution of emissions to the point or country of fossil-fuel extraction instead of where emissions are produced or consumed, with the scope (CO2 only vs fuel-combustion GHGs) differing by source.

Different ways of attributing or integrating facility-level emissions in an inventory: purchase-share allocation to a buyer (corporate Scope 3) versus integration into national inventories by industry classification (IPCC).
Check comparing feedstock supply in national fuel statistics with process feedstock requirements (SFC × production) in the inventory, given in two IPCC guideline editions.
Differing IPCC usages of feedstock: fossil fuel used as a raw material in chemical conversion versus the total input material to a manufacturing process.
The term feedstock appears either as fossil fuel used as raw material or as total process input material, depending on the IPCC section.
Alternative initial splitting rules for disaggregating FIGARO supply values into EXIOBASE industries and products.

Different sources define the boundary of final consumption differently (households only, households plus government and NPISHs, community needs), which matters for consumption-based carbon responsibility.
Different statistical definitions of final consumption, with differing scope, which matter for consumption-based responsibility and energy physical-quantity corrections.
Different definitions of final consumption: national-accounts expenditure (SNA, handbook) versus household-only energy end use (SEEA), relevant to consumption-based carbon responsibility boundaries.
Family of first-order decay formulations for landfill CH4 that differ in decay timing, delay convention and aggregation.
Time for a carbon or organic pool to lose half its mass under first-order decay, with different pools and relations to the rate constant (HWP via ESL, waste via k).
Variants of the first-order decay model for CH4 from solid waste disposal that differ in delay timing and inventory-level aggregation.
Exponential decay models used in IPCC guidelines to estimate carbon stock or emissions release over time for waste and wood product pools.
The yr^-1 rate constant k of first-order decay used for different carbon pools (HWP, solid waste disposal).
The first-order decay constant in yr^-1 used for carbon or waste pools, defined via half-life in HWP and as a reaction rate constant in solid waste disposal.
IPCC glossary definitions of flaring as burning of waste gas streams without useful energy use, with wording differences between 2006 and 2019.
Definitions of flaring in IPCC 2006 and 2019 glossaries and fugitive-emission chapters, differing in whether liquids and incinerators are included and whether disposal purpose is stated.
IPCC 2006 and 2019 definitions of flooded land as water bodies whose surface area has been changed by human activity, with the 2019 version broader.
By-product (e.g. CF4, C2F6) emissions formed from input gas consumption, with variants in heel handling, abatement term and process-type summation.
Competing threshold definitions of forest: the fixed FAO values of 0.5 ha, 5 m and 10% canopy, and the country-selected ranges of 0.05-1.0 ha, 2-5 m and 10-30%.
Different area, height and canopy-cover criteria used to define forest or forest land across IPCC, FAO/JAXA and SEEA sources.
An agreement to trade a quantity at an agreed price on a future date, defined in the national accounts and in carbon-market contexts.

n: Fossil CO2 from waste incineration and open burning
s: Two IPCC 2006 ways of estimating fossil CO2 from waste combustion, based either on waste-type amounts or on MSW composition.

n: Fossil CO2 from waste incineration/open burning
s: Carbon-mass-balance estimates of fossil CO2 from burning waste, computed either per waste type or from MSW composition fractions.
Share of managed manure N volatilised as NH3 and NOx in a manure management system, expressed as a percent in 2006 and as a dimensionless fraction in 2019.
The Tier 1 default fraction of N lost by leaching and runoff, set differently in the 2006 Guidelines (0.30) and 2019 Refinement (0.24).
Alternative ETS rules for distributing allowances free of charge, by historical emissions or by output-based benchmarks.
Rules for allocating free emission allowances in a trading system: grandparenting on historical emissions or benchmarking on output.

Different sources define 'fugitive emissions' with different scopes (fuel chain only vs. also non-fuel facility sources, intentional vs. unintentional releases, and a halogenated-gas production sense).

Definitions of fugitive emissions that differ in scope: organisational facility leaks (GHG Protocol), the fossil fuel chain (IPCC), including or excluding venting and flaring, and sector-specific uses.
Standardized exchange-traded forward-type contract, used for financial instruments in the SNA and for allowances or offsets in emissions trading.

n: FWTW debt securities stock table layouts
s: The same illustrative from-whom-to-whom debt securities stock data shown as an issuer-by-holder matrix and as a time series.
Estimate carbon stock change in a pool as average annual gains (increment or inputs) minus losses, with pool-specific variants for biomass, dead wood and litter.

n: Gas-specific emission factor EF_i,f at 100% control uptime
s: Facility-level emission factor for FC input gas i at full control uptime, either measurement-derived (6.23b) or a maximum default (6.23c).
The average gas-to-oil ratio (m3/m3 at 15 °C and 101.325 kPa) as defined in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Benchmark carbon-intensity values for electricity in physical units, which differ between 表39 (821) and 表28 (630).
GDP can be computed on the production, income or expenditure side. The three give the same total but offer different allocation perspectives.
GDP computed as the sum of income components (employee compensation, operating surplus, mixed income and net production/import taxes).
GDP can be measured from the production, income or expenditure side, and the three measures are identical in the SNA.
The five principles (relevance, completeness, consistency, transparency, accuracy) that GHG Protocol standards require inventories to follow.

n: GHG climate impact measure (CO2-eq) in GRO24
s: The GRO24 measure of GHG-based climate impact in CO2-equivalents, given as concept, method, per-capita and consumption/production-perspective forms with different units.

n: GHG emissions allocation (partitioning among outputs, co-products or users)
s: Different GHG Protocol standards and guidance define allocation as partitioning or assigning emissions or responsibility among outputs, co-products or users, with different boundaries.
Different sources define which gases count as GHGs: six, seven, three, or a broader IPCC 2019 list.
Different sources define the set of greenhouse gases in scope differently: six gases, seven gases including NF3, or the broader IPCC 2019 Refinement list.
Documentation plan for data sources, boundary, calculation methods and QA/QC of a GHG inventory, defined for corporate Scope 3 and for product inventories.
GHG Protocol rules that prevent the same emissions from being counted twice across scopes, companies or lessor/lessee pairs.
Location-based and market-based ways of calculating scope 2 emissions from purchased electricity, illustrated by worked examples.
IPCC tiered approaches for estimating CO2 from glass production, from default factors to carbonate-input accounting.
IPCC 2006 tiered approaches for estimating glass production CO2: default factor, process-level factors, and carbonate inputs.
Definitions of GWP as a radiative forcing ratio relative to CO2, differing in whether a time horizon is stated (IPCC glossary 'e.g., 100 years', AR6 GWP100, GHG Protocol unspecified).
Factor expressing the radiative forcing of a GHG relative to CO2, used to convert gases into CO2e, defined in IPCC, GHG Protocol, GRI, GPC and IFRS-related sources.
GWP is the factor expressing the radiative forcing of a GHG relative to CO2, which is used to convert emissions to CO2e.
GNI is GDP adjusted for primary incomes receivable from and payable to the rest of the world, with slightly different wording in SNA and Eora.
The IPCC definition of good practice, with 2006 and 2019 wordings that differ slightly.

Good practice is the IPCC set of procedures ensuring inventories contain neither over- nor under-estimates and have uncertainties reduced as far as practicable, with the 2019 Refinement wording differing from 2006.
IPCC concept of inventory accuracy without systematic over- or under-estimation and with reduced uncertainty, with wording differing between the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
IPCC definitions of the grassland land category across the 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement, differing in scope and forest-threshold wording.
IPCC 2006 and 2019 Refinement define the grassland land category with different wording and scope.
Estimating interprovincial or interregional trade flows with gravity-type models using supply, demand and distance, often followed by RAS balancing.

n: Gravity model for interregional trade flows
s: Gravity-type estimation of interregional commodity flows from supply, demand and distance, with different specifications and calibration in different China MRIO sources.
SNA 2025 and SEEA 2012 define gross capital formation with slightly different components, with valuables included in SNA and not mentioned in SEEA.

n: Gross operating surplus and mixed income derivation
s: Gross operating surplus and gross mixed income can be derived as a production-side residual or by summing income-based components.
GVA is estimated by production, income or cost-based approaches, and the identities use different component sets.
GVA can be valued at basic prices, producers' prices or factor cost, which treat product and production taxes and subsidies differently.
GVA valued at basic prices or at producers' prices, which differ in the treatment of product taxes and subsidies.
The word 'gross' denotes different conventions across sources: inclusion of recycling or non-energy flows, exclusion of offsets, or recording of all flows. Each has its own boundary meaning.
Conversion of non-CO2 gases to CO2-eq depends on the chosen metric (GWP100, GWP*) and the IPCC assessment report supplying the values.

n: GWP time horizon and assessment report convention
s: Rules for converting greenhouse gases to CO2e with GWP values, differing by assessment report (SAR, AR4, AR5, AR6), horizon (100-year or 20-year) and disclosure requirement.
The time for half of a decaying material pool (waste carbon or harvested wood product carbon) to be lost.
HWP treatment across the 2006 IPCC Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement, kept as separate versions.
Different source definitions of harvested wood products and where they place the boundary.
Different framework-specific definitions of HWP as the carbon pool or reservoir in harvested wood, differing in what is excluded and which accounting scope applies.
Definitions of hazardous waste that differ in scope between the SEEA framework and the IPCC waste guidance.
Legislator-defined general characterisation (SEEA) versus enumerated waste types (IPCC) of hazardous waste.

n: HFC-23 by-product emission estimation from HCFC-22 production
s: Tiered IPCC methods for estimating HFC-23 emissions from HCFC-22 production, from default-factor to plant-level calculations.
The IPCC carbon-balance-efficiency formula for HFC-23 emission factors in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: HFC-23 emission estimation from HCFC-22 production
s: Tiered IPCC ways of estimating by-product HFC-23 emissions from HCFC-22 production, from default factors to plant-level data.
HFC-23 emission factor derived from fluorine balance efficiency in HCFC-22 production, in 2006 and 2019 versions.
Alternative ways to estimate HFC-23 emissions from a process stream: direct measurement (concentration × flow × time) or a scaled standard emission factor.
Estimating HFC-23 emissions from monitored HFC-23 concentration in HCFC-22 reactor product, in different formulations across IPCC editions.
Matrix mapping HFC and PFC chemicals to ODS-substitute application areas, as given in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: HFC/PFC use distribution by application area
s: Example shares of HFC/PFC use across application areas, with different years and country groupings in the 2006 and 2019 sources.

n: Higher-tier use for key categories (good practice)
s: Good-practice statements that Tier 2 or 3 should be used where a category is key, stated generally and for grassland biomass.

n: Historical HWP data and initial stock handling
s: Edition-specific treatments of the missing early HWP history: 2006 estimates of pre-1961 production and trade, and the 2019 initial-stock approximation that replaces it.

Definitions of household final consumption expenditure given in SNA 2025, the Supply-Use Handbook (quoting 2008 SNA) and SEEA 2012, with differing emphasis on imputation, residency and goods acquired abroad.

n: HVAE CF4 emission estimation methods (aluminium smelting)
s: Alternative Tier 2/3 methods for CF4 from high-voltage anode effects: slope, Marks and Nunez, and Dion et al.
Tier 2 approaches for estimating PFC emissions from high-voltage anode effects in aluminium smelting: the slope method and the Dion et al. per-event method.
Alternative accounting approaches for carbon in harvested wood products, differing in system boundary and in which country reports fluxes.
Alternative perspectives for attributing harvested wood product carbon: domestic consumption (stock-change) versus domestic harvest (production).
Default density, carbon fraction and carbon conversion factors for converting harvested wood product quantities to carbon, across 2006 and 2019 editions.
Accounting for harvested wood product carbon where flows are attributed by domestic consumption, presented in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement with different formula presentations.

n: Hybrid method for purchased goods emissions (Scope 3)
s: Scope 3 purchased-goods calculations that combine supplier-specific data with secondary data, in variants that depend on which supplier data are available.
Family of 2019 Refinement tiered equations for CO2 from hydrogen production by feedstock carbon, net of recovered CO2 (and stored carbon at Tier 3).

n: Hydrogen production CO2 estimation by tier
s: Alternative tiered carbon-content-based methods for CO2 from hydrogen production, from output-based (1b) to plant-level (2/3) forms.
Measurement of the implicit service charge on loans and deposits as the margin between bank interest and reference-rate (SNA) interest, with sector-specific forms.
Dividing use tables by source (local, interregional, international or by country) assuming identical user distribution across sources.
Assumption that the share of demand met by imports or other regions is applied proportionally to demand categories when building IO tables.
Methods that split intermediate/final demand into domestically and externally supplied parts using an import share or coefficient.
Allocation of emissions to the suppliers of primary inputs (value added or income) via downstream Ghosh-type tracing, as opposed to production or consumption allocation.
Carbon responsibility allocated by primary input or income through supply-driven Ghosh-type linkages instead of demand-driven Leontief linkages.

n: Independent third-party review of emissions information
s: Review of reported emissions or inventory information by a party independent of the compiler, which appears as GHG Protocol assurance (corporate and product) and as ETS verification.

n: Indicative anthropogenic CH4 from flooded land
s: Indicative anthropogenic CH4 share of flooded land emissions, excluding unmanaged waterbodies, for the >20-year (7.16) and <=20-year (7.18) reservoir classes.
Emissions attributed to an entity or sector that physically occur elsewhere, with scope varying by source (all value-chain emissions versus electricity/heat reallocation only).
Different sources use 'indirect emissions' with different boundaries, from other-company sources (GHG Protocol) to electricity and heat reallocation (IPCC AR6 scope 2).
Emissions that result from a reporting company's activities but occur at sources owned or controlled by another company, as defined in GHG Protocol documents.
N2O emitted after nitrogen leaves its original source via atmospheric deposition or leaching/runoff, with differing boundaries across IPCC 2006 and 2019 materials.

n: Indirect N2O from managed soils (volatilisation/deposition and leaching/runoff pathways)
s: Indirect N2O from managed soils via volatilised-N redeposition (EF4) and leached or run-off N (EF5), expressed in IPCC Tier 1 as N2O-N and in the community protocol as tonnes of N2O.
Default methane correction factors for industrial wastewater treatment pathways, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
Alternative technology or sales-structure assumptions (models C and D) for deriving industry-by-industry input-output tables from supply-use tables.
A group of establishments classified by the same or similar productive activity, defined slightly differently in SNA, SEEA and the supply-use handbook.
The SUT-to-IOT transformation assumption that each industry has its own production structure irrespective of its product mix.

n: Inorganic soil carbon change zero default
s: Default assumption that inorganic soil carbon stock change is zero outside Tier 3 approaches, stated in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Balance, year-specificity and technology-assumption rules governing how IOTs are derived from SUTs and used in MRIO-based accounting.
A good that is an input to further production and is not consumed in its current form by the end user, defined slightly differently across the GHG Protocol standards.
Different standards define 'intermediate product' from the producer's, product life-cycle or seller's perspective (further-processed inputs vs sold products whose use-phase is accounted downstream).

Alternative conventions for assigning international transport (bunker) fuel and emissions: excluded from national totals as a memo item (IPCC), by flight-stage departure/landing, or attributed to the operator's country of residence (SEEA/Handbook).

n: Interregional trade matrix estimation for MRIO
s: Alternative procedures for estimating interregional trade flows for multi-regional input-output tables.
The line or scope that delimits which emissions an inventory covers, defined by consolidation approach in corporate standards or by gases, sources, geography and time in community standards.
Different definitions of what an inventory boundary encloses: organization-based (consolidation approach, operational boundaries) versus community/geography-based (gases, sources, area, time span).
GHG accounting standards define the inventory boundary either by organizational/operational boundaries or by geographic area, gases and time span.
Acquisition and compilation of activity data for national GHG inventories, as defined in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: Inventory quality assurance and quality control
s: Procedures for assessing and maintaining the quality of GHG inventories, in IPCC 2006 and 2019 versions and in the GHG Protocol corporate data management plan.

n: Inventory recalculation on methodology or data change
s: Different standards and guidelines require recalculating base year or time-series emissions when methods, data sources, models or boundaries change significantly, with differing triggers and exclusions.
Qualitative codes used in GHG inventory tables to explain missing, excluded or confidential entries, with different key sets in the IPCC Guidelines and the GPC.
Ways of assigning emissions to investors or capital owners, either via capital-owner investment choices or via equity-share scope 3 Category 15.
The multiplicative IPAT equation and Herendeen's logarithmic form for attributing impact changes to population, affluence and technology.
Decomposition of environmental impact into population, affluence and technology drivers, in multiplicative or logarithmic form.

n: IPCC 2006 GL Vol.3 Annex 1 Tier 1 HFC calculation example
s: Excel calculation examples for HFC emissions from ODS substitutes (refrigeration, HFC country data, fire protection). They are IPCC inventory-style worked examples, not carbon-responsibility accounting.
Standard IPCC national inventory reporting table templates (trend, sectoral, background) published in 2006 and updated in the 2019 Refinement, here only as blank templates.
Recommended category and gas aggregation levels for Approach 1 key category analysis, issued in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Category-level uncertainty combination by simple error propagation for a single year and for the trend, as stated in the 2006 Guidelines and the updated 2019 worksheet.

n: IPCC Approach 2 Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis
s: Uncertainty estimation by sampling input PDFs over many iterations, described in the 2006 Guidelines and referenced or illustrated in the 2019 Refinement.

n: IPCC below-ground to above-ground biomass ratio R
s: Root-to-shoot ratio tables for forest biomass in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement update.
The IPCC checklist form for category-specific quality control, issued in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
The Cropland land-use category as defined across IPCC 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement.
IPCC sectoral reporting table for the Energy sector in the 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement versions.
Expert judgement is used in IPCC inventory guidance to choose methods and input data, fill gaps and judge uncertainty.

n: IPCC guidance on higher-tier methods for key categories
s: The IPCC recommendation to use Tier 2/3 methods for key categories, stated in two guideline versions that differ in the Tier 1 fallback condition.

n: IPCC harvested wood products production approach
s: IPCC HWP accounting approach that attributes carbon in wood products to the country of domestic harvest, across 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement versions.

n: IPCC HWP worksheet country input layout
s: Country-level year-by-product input sheets of the IPCC harvested wood products worksheet, including demo and test copies that share one column layout.

n: IPCC inventory guideline editions and volume structure
s: Volume and chapter organisation of the 2006 IPCC Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement, kept as separate editions with their own update notes.
Procedures and operational rules, in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement, for identifying categories that most influence a national inventory by level, trend and uncertainty.
Approach 1 ranks categories by level and trend contribution to the inventory. Approach 2 additionally weights by category uncertainty.
Three IPCC ways of representing land-use area and change (net totals, conversion matrices, spatially explicit), described in both the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Three levels of land-use area data in the IPCC AFOLU volume: net change only, gross conversions without spatial explicitness, and spatially explicit tracking through time.

n: IPCC land-use area uncertainty by Approach (Table 3.7)
s: Indicative uncertainty of land-use area under Approaches 1 to 3, given as text ranges in the 2006 and 2019 versions.

n: IPCC list of fuels usable as chemical feedstock or reductant
s: IPCC list of fossil fuels considered for feedstock/reductant balance, in 2006 and 2019 Refinement versions.

n: IPCC manure management CH4 emission factor table
s: Default manure-management CH4 emission factor tables with different units and structure in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement.

n: IPCC memo items outside national totals
s: Emission and removal items reported in the IPCC reporting tables as memo or information rows that are not added to the national inventory total, relevant to boundary and double-counting checks.
IPCC levels of methodological complexity, from Tier 1 (basic/default) to Tier 3 (most demanding), used in both the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement, in generic and sector-specific forms.

n: IPCC MSW generation and management default data (Table 2A.1)
s: Default municipal solid waste generation rates and management fractions by country and region, published in the 2006 Guidelines (year 2000) and the 2019 Refinement (year 2010).
The 2006 IPCC Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement are two versions of IPCC national GHG inventory guidance that are used together, with the Refinement supplementing but not replacing the 2006 text.

n: IPCC reporting Short Summary Table B
s: Condensed national summary reporting table at the level of IPCC sector headings, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
National emissions and removals summary reporting table by sector and gas, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
IPCC inventory rules that assign each emission to a single sector by subtracting or excluding quantities reported elsewhere.

n: IPCC stationary combustion default emission factors (Volume 2 Ch.2)
s: Tier 1 default CO2, CH4 and N2O emission factors for fuels in stationary combustion, split by source category (kg/TJ NCV).

n: IPCC Tier 1 abandoned underground mine CH4
s: Tier 1 global-average estimation of methane from abandoned underground coal mines, with different equation structures in the 2006 and 2019 versions.

n: IPCC Tier 1 applicability for iron and steel production
s: The IPCC condition that Tier 1 is suitable only when iron and steel production is not a key category, as stated in the 2006 and 2019 editions.
Sector-specific conditions under which the simplest Tier 1 method may be used, such as non-key sources, last resort, or no company data.

n: IPCC Tier 1 biomass carbon change on land conversion (Eq 2.15/2.16)
s: Tier 1 biomass carbon change when land is converted, as area times the difference between biomass carbon before and after conversion, with land-use-specific assumptions.

n: IPCC Tier 1 CO2 from pig iron, DRI, sinter and pellet
s: Tier 1 non-energy CO2 for pig iron, DRI, sinter and pellets as activity quantity times a default emission factor, grouped in 2006 and split into separate equations in 2019.

n: IPCC Tier 1 default CO2 emission factors for iron and steel production
s: Default per-tonne CO2 factors for iron and steel production routes, published in different IPCC editions (2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement) whose values must be kept version-specific.
The simplest IPCC inventory tier, which estimates emissions from activity data and default factors, with sector-specific definitions.

n: IPCC Tier 1 iron and steel CO2 (BOF/EAF/OHF)
s: Tier 1 non-energy CO2 from steelmaking as production by process times a default EF, as published in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Example climate, soil, ecological-zone and management strata for Tier 1 land emissions estimation, in the 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement versions.

n: IPCC Tier 1 pig iron, DRI, sinter and pellet CO2 (activity x EF)
s: Tier 1 CO2 for pig iron, DRI, sinter and pellet production as national activity times a default EF, presented in combined (2006) and separate (2019) equations.
Tier 1 CO2 from steelmaking as the sum of BOF, EAF and OHF crude steel output times default emission factors, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
Across IPCC guidance, Tier 2 means the Tier 1 structure applied with country- or region-specific data and factors; the scope differs by sector.

n: IPCC Tier 2 country- or technology-specific estimation level
s: Tier 2 as an intermediate IPCC level between Tier 1 defaults and Tier 3 facility-specific or model-based estimation, using country- or technology-specific data.
In IPCC inventory guidelines, Tier 2 means applying the Tier 1 approach with country- or region-specific data, defined slightly differently per sector.

Several sector-specific methods labelled Tier 2b in the IPCC Guidelines. Their parameterisation differs by sector and edition: electronics 2006 versus 2019, textile wet processes, and ODS-substitute mass balance.
The highest-detail IPCC inventory tier, defined with sector- and edition-specific wording as facility-, plant- or process-specific data, measurement or modelling.
The highest-detail IPCC tier, using facility-level, model-based or measurement-based data, with category-specific wording.
The highest IPCC methodological tier, using facility-specific, measured or model-based data. The exact definition varies by sector and edition.
IPCC chapters define Tier 1/Tier 2 by different criteria (default factors, country-specific data, data aggregation, throughput-based default EFs), so the term has no single global meaning.
Sector- and context-specific statements of what Tier 1, 2 and 3 mean in IPCC guidance, differing in whether tiers are defined by factor granularity, activity basis or pathway coverage.
IPCC tiers of increasing methodological complexity and data requirements for estimating emissions, from default factors to models and plant-level measurements.
Sector-specific definitions of Tier 1/2/3 inventory methods, in which higher tiers use more country-, technology- or facility-specific data.
IPCC inventory methods are organised into Tier 1/2/3 levels of increasing data specificity, defined differently per sector.

n: IPCC uncertainty combination approaches (Approach 1 error propagation / Approach 2 Monte Carlo)
s: Two ways to combine category uncertainties into national total and trend uncertainty: analytic error propagation and Monte Carlo simulation, in both the 2006 and 2019 editions.
The Waste volume of the IPCC guidelines, with different chapter structure in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
The IPCC Table 4 reporting template for waste, in the 2006 Guidelines index and the 2019 Refinement.

n: IPPU and Energy sector boundary conventions for industrial combustion
s: Different sources assign combustion and process emissions of industrial plants to either IPPU or Energy, which changes inventory and intensity boundaries.

n: IPPU CO2 completeness check for non-energy fuel use
s: Checks comparing reported IPPU CO2 with the potential CO2 of carbon in fuels used for non-energy purposes, across IPCC editions.
The 2006 IPCC IPPU sector definition and its updated 2019 Refinement classification structure.
IPCC rules for avoiding double counting of emissions between the industrial-process and energy sectors for petrochemical and carbon black processes.

n: Iron and steel and sinter Tier 2 carbon mass balance
s: Carbon mass-balance CO2 estimates for iron and steel and sinter production, with sign conventions and terms that differ between the 2006 and 2019 versions.

n: Iron and steel Tier 2 carbon mass balance (Equation 4.9)
s: Tier 2 carbon mass balance for non-energy CO2 from iron and steel, which differs in term signs between the 2006 and 2019 editions.
Successive revisions of the UN ISIC industry classification used to define sector dimensions.

n: 京都议定书温室气体清单
s: Lists of Kyoto Protocol gases covered by corporate accounting standards. The versions give different counts.
Permission for an entity, or the affected part of it, to follow a jurisdiction- or exchange-mandated GWP set or GHG measurement method instead of the IFRS S2 default.
Multiplicative decomposition of emissions into driver factors, here an agricultural form and an energy-sector form.
Multiplicative identities that split emissions into drivers: the energy-system form for CO2 and the agricultural form for AFOLU emissions.
Multiplicative identities that split emissions into driver factors, with an energy-based CO2 form and a land-based AFOLU form.
Systematic identification of key categories using Approach 1 or 2 level and trend assessments, in the 2006 and 2019 guideline versions.
The IPCC procedures, thresholds and notation keys for identifying key categories by level, trend and qualitative criteria under Approach 1 and Approach 2, in 2006 and 2019 versions.
IPCC 2006 methods for identifying key inventory categories, differing in threshold (95% vs 90%) and in whether uncertainty is included.

Inventory categories prioritised because they significantly influence a national total in level, trend or uncertainty, defined in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement with minor wording differences.
Different uses of the term 'key sector': a judgemental group of industries of special interest (SNA) versus a linkage-based formula (input-output).
The term 'key sector' is used with different meanings: a linkage-based criterion in input-output analysis and a selected group of industries in SNA thematic accounts.
Different IPCC 2006 and 2019 definitions and reporting categories for land converted to cropland.

n: Land converted to cropland (IPCC inventory category)
s: The IPCC inventory category for land converted to cropland, appearing with different reporting codes and conventions in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: Land converted to flooded land definitions
s: IPCC 2006 and 2019 definitions of the flooded-land category, with and without a 20-year window.
Different formulations of the category 'Land converted to Forest Land' across IPCC 2006 Chapter 4 and the 2019 Refinement.
Variant IPCC definitions of land converted to forest: transition period, afforestation/reforestation, and the default 20-year window.
Definitions of land cover as the observed physical and biological cover of the surface, in SNA 2025 and the IPCC 2006 glossary.

n: Land use and land cover definitions
s: Definitions of land use and land cover that differ across the IPCC, SNA and SEEA sources.

Conventions that decide in which period or category land-use change emissions are attributed: 20-year amortization (product), 20-year transition (national inventory), report in new category (community).
Rules for spreading land-use change impacts over 20 years of production, with different treatment for annual and semi-annual crops.
Different class systems for dividing land into use categories, namely the SEEA interim classification and the IPCC six-category AFOLU scheme, with no crosswalk in the catalog.
Several differently worded definitions of 'land use' in SEEA, SNA 2025 and the IPCC 2006 and 2019 glossaries.
Fraction of methane in landfill gas with differing stated default values or ranges across sources.
Laspeyres-type price and volume indices that weight changes by fixed reference-period quantities or prices.
The matrix inverse capturing direct and indirect requirements per unit of final demand, written with different notations across the MRIO and SUT/IO sources.
The input-output relation x = (I−A)^-1 y linking gross output to final demand, expressed with varying notation across sources.
Assessment of the inputs, outputs and environmental impacts of a product or service across its life stages.
Emission factors that cover upstream and other life-cycle stages beyond direct combustion.
IPCC tiered approaches for estimating CO2 from lime production, from default factors to plant-specific carbonate inputs.

n: Linear interpolation for time-series gap filling
s: Filling missing intermediate years in an inventory time series by interpolating between detailed estimates, in the 2006 and 2019 IPCC versions.
Scope 2 accounting based on average emission intensity of the grids where energy is consumed, as defined in the GHG Protocol and GRI.
Estimating CO2 emissions from lubricant use from consumption, carbon content and ODU factor, at Tier 1 (single default) and Tier 2 (per type) level.
Estimation of CO2 from lubricant use by multiplying consumption, carbon content, ODU factor and 44/12, either with aggregate defaults (Tier 1) or by lubricant type (Tier 2).

Bottom-up mobile air conditioning refrigerant emissions as the sum of container, charging, lifetime, servicing and end-of-life emissions, presented as worked examples in the 2006 and 2019 IPCC guidance.
IPCC definition of managed land as land with human interventions for production, ecological or social functions, used in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Managed manure nitrogen available for soil application, feed, fuel or construction, computed from livestock excretion net of system losses plus bedding N, in the 2006 and 2019 IPCC guidance versions.
Tiered IPCC approaches to on-site CO2-C emissions from peat extraction areas.

n: Manure CH4 emission factor (VS, B0, MCF)
s: The IPCC Tier 2 CH4 emission factor for manure, built from volatile solids, B0, MCF and system fractions, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
Nitrogen lost by leaching and runoff from managed manure, with the loss fraction in % in 2006 and as a dimensionless fraction in 2019.

n: Manure management N leaching and runoff loss
s: Estimation of nitrogen lost by leaching and runoff from manure management systems, with versions differing in unit convention and co-digestate terms.

n: Manure management NH3/NOx volatilisation N loss
s: Nitrogen lost as NH3 and NOx from managed manure, calculated from head count, N excretion, system share and a volatilisation fraction, defined differently in 2006 and 2019.
Category definitions of manure management systems used to key MCF, EF3 and N loss defaults, in 2006 and 2019 editions.

n: Manure N loss fraction in management systems (Frac_LossMS)
s: Fraction of managed manure nitrogen lost in a management system, whose component losses and units differ between IPCC 2006 and IPCC 2019.
Total manure nitrogen loss fraction in manure management systems, expressed in percent in 2006 and as a dimensionless component sum in 2019.
Fraction of manure nitrogen lost as NH3 and NOx in manure management systems, defined on different bases and units across IPCC versions.
Variants of the NH3+NOx volatilisation fraction in manure management systems, differing in unit (% versus fraction) and denominator (managed N versus excreted N).

Allocation of electricity-related emissions to consumers through contractual instruments and supplier-specific or residual-mix factors, defined with different boundaries in corporate and community-scale protocols.

n: Mass-balance approach for ODS substitute (refrigerant) emissions
s: Mass-balance estimation of refrigerant emissions from new sales, new equipment charge, retiring equipment charge and destruction, at sub-application level (Tier 2b).
Maximum methane yield per unit of organic input, defined on different bases for livestock manure (kg VS) and wastewater (kg BOD/COD).
The theoretical maximum CH4 yield per unit of organic matter, defined per BOD/COD for wastewater and per volatile solids for livestock manure, in different guideline versions.
Theoretical maximum methane yield per unit of degradable organic substrate, defined per volatile solids for manure and per BOD or COD for wastewater.

n: Maximum managed land area basis for stock-difference recalculation
s: When managed land area changes, carbon stocks are recalculated over the whole time series using the maximum managed area, so area additions are not counted as stock increases.
Good-practice requirement that measured inventory data be representative and obtained with a suitable, preferably standardised, method, in the IPCC 2006 and 2019 versions.
IPCC convention of reporting certain emissions outside the national inventory total, in the 2006 and 2019 reporting tables.

Trade in which goods are bought from one foreign party and resold to another, with definitions differing in whether the territory test is the compiling economy, the owner's territory or the merchant's home border.

n: Metallurgical coke CO2 estimation by tier
s: Alternative tiered methods (production-based EF, simplified carbon balance, full carbon mass balance) for CO2 from metallurgical coke production.
IPCC factors that adjust CH4 potential for treatment, management or disposal conditions, with different definitions and units in the livestock, solid-waste and wastewater sectors.

n: Methane conversion factor for manure management (MCF)
s: System- and climate-specific percentage of the maximum methane capacity B0 realised in manure management, as defined in the 2006 and 2019 livestock chapters.
Share of gross energy intake converted to enteric methane, defined in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: Methane conversion factor Ym (IPCC enteric fermentation)
s: The percentage of gross energy intake converted to methane in ruminant enteric fermentation, as defined in the 2006 IPCC Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: Methane correction factor for solid waste disposal sites (SWDS MCF)
s: Dimensionless factor adjusting CH4 generation by SWDS management type, with different default values in the 2006 and 2019 IPCC volumes and the community protocol.

n: Methane correction factor for wastewater treatment (MCF)
s: Fraction describing how anaerobic a wastewater treatment or discharge pathway is, defined either as share of B0 realised or as share of organics treated anaerobically.
The CH4 share of landfill gas, given with different default values or ranges by IPCC 2006 and the community protocol.

n: Mineral soil carbon change on land conversion (Equation 2.25)
s: Worksheets by destination land-use category that all point to Equation 2.25 Formulation B for mineral soil carbon change, without reproducing the formula.

n: Minimum cross-entropy balancing for MRIO construction
s: Cross-entropy minimisation used to balance provincial IOTs and interprovincial trade matrices against control totals while staying close to the initial structure.
Cross-entropy minimisation used in the interprovincial MRIO source to balance rows, columns, or the trade flow matrix under different constraints.
Minimum content that standards require for reporting or exchanging emissions, product footprints or statistical releases; the scopes and purposes differ.
Alternative reference bases against which a community or organisation expresses an emission reduction goal: base-year absolute, base-year intensity, or baseline scenario.
Emissions from fuel combustion in transport equipment, framed as an IPCC inventory category or a GHG Protocol corporate source category.
Source-specific definitions of 'model' and 'model uncertainty' across IPCC 2006, IPCC 2019 and GHG Protocol standards, kept as separate versions.

n: Model uncertainty (GHG accounting and inventory definitions)
s: Uncertainty from modelling limitations, defined with different emphasis by the GHG Protocol standards, product standard and IPCC inventory guidance.
Uncertainty from limitations of mathematical or modelling approaches used to estimate emissions, defined with different wording in IPCC and GHG Protocol sources.
Ratio of the monetary value of an input (domestic intermediate, imported intermediate or primary input) used by sector j to the output value of sector j.
Allocation of emissions to regions/sectors using multi-regional input-output models, with variants differing in the allocation basis (final demand vs. primary input/income).

Information on what MRIO data must be harmonised, structured and documented before regional carbon responsibility accounting; sources cover different aspects and none gives the complete specification.

n: MRIO data structure and regional dimensions
s: Structural choices (supply-use vs I–O blocks, enterprise subsegments, subnational compilation) that determine how multi-regional input-output data are organised.
Input-output tables linking multiple regions or countries through explicit inter-regional trade flows, in province-level and international forms.
Wet-weight basis and reference year of IPCC default MSW generation data, which differ between the 2006 Guidelines (year 2000) and 2019 Refinement (year 2010).
Treating co-products or exports by expanding the system and substituting equivalent product emissions.
IPCC rules on whether and where multi-year averaging may replace best annual estimates, differing between 2006 GL and 2019 Refinement.

n: N2O emissions from centralized wastewater treatment plants
s: N2O emitted at centralized wastewater treatment plants, estimated either per capita (2006 Equation 6.9) or from nitrogen load by pathway (2019 worksheet).
Tier 1 emission-factor and Tier 3 flue-gas-measurement approaches to N2O emissions from waste incineration.
Different scopes and thresholds used to define which AFOLU disturbances count as natural (non-anthropogenic) in inventories.
Definitions of what counts as natural resources, which differ between environmental-economic accounting (SEEA) and national accounts (SNA) in their ownership and economic-value conditions.

n: NE_wool estimation (livestock net energy for wool)
s: Net energy needed for wool production, estimated from wool energy value and annual wool production, with differing daily-conversion treatment across IPCC guideline versions.

n: Net consumption of a chemical in an application
s: Production plus imports minus exports minus destruction for an ODS-substitute application, in the 2006 and 2019 guideline versions.
Net embodied emissions moved between regions or countries through trade, with different scales, units and sign conventions in each source.
Net greenhouse-gas emissions as gross emissions adjusted by removals or credits, defined differently in IPCC inventory and community-scale GPC contexts.
