Different accounting conventions that call a netted emissions quantity 'net emissions', with different items netted against gross emissions.
Different meanings of 'net emissions' across standards: sources minus sink removals versus gross emissions adjusted for carbon credits.
Different definitions of balancing residual emissions against removals or offsets: CO2 only, all GHGs weighted by GWP100, or city-scale neutrality allowing offsetting.
Different definitions of balancing residual emissions against removals or offsets, varying in gas scope, metric and permitted cancellation mechanisms.

n: Nitric acid N2O emission estimation tiers
s: IPCC Tier 1 and Tier 2 estimation methods for N2O from nitric acid production, differing in technology disaggregation and abatement treatment.
IPCC tiered approaches for estimating N2O from nitric acid production, from technology defaults to plant-level measurement.

n: Non-energy use of fossil fuels (IPCC versions)
s: IPCC 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement define fossil-fuel non-energy use (feedstock, reductant, non-energy products) with versioned wording that must be tracked separately.
Variants of SNA 2025 non-life insurance output as premiums earned plus premium supplements minus adjusted claims, differing in how adjusted claims are determined.
Definitions of shall, should and may that distinguish requirements, recommendations and options in GHG standards.

n: Notation keys for incomplete or excluded inventory data
s: Qualitative codes used in GHG inventory reporting to mark missing, included-elsewhere, confidential or non-occurring entries.
Qualitative keys used in inventory reporting tables to mark missing, included-elsewhere, confidential, not-applicable or non-occurring entries.

n: Offset reporting and double-counting treatment in disclosure standards
s: Rules in different disclosure standards for reporting offsets separately and avoiding double counting.

n: Oil and gas segment general emission equations (activity × EF)
s: Segment-by-segment sums of activity data times emission factors for fugitive emissions in oil, natural gas and coal exploration, production, processing, transport and distribution.

n: Oil production CH4 flaring emissions, Alternative Tier 2 (Eq. 4.2.4)
s: CH4 emitted from flaring at oil production, in the IPCC 2006 and 2019 editions.

n: Oil production CO2 flaring emissions, Alternative Tier 2 (Eq. 4.2.5)
s: CO2 from flaring at oil production, including formation CO2 and CO2 from oxidation of CH4 and NMVOC with a soot correction, in the IPCC 2006 and 2019 editions.

n: Oil production N2O flaring emissions, Alternative Tier 2 (Eq. 4.2.8)
s: N2O from flaring at oil production using an N2O emission factor, in the IPCC 2006 and 2019 editions.

n: Oil production venting emissions, Alternative Tier 2 (Eq. 4.2.3)
s: Mass-balance estimate of venting emissions at oil production from GOR, oil output, conservation efficiency and flared fraction, given in both IPCC 2006 and 2019 editions.
IPCC tiered approaches to estimating on-site CO2-C emissions from managed peatlands under peat extraction.
A contract giving the buyer the right but not the obligation to buy or sell an item at a predetermined price.
Criteria for classifying soils as organic, expressed in IPCC sources as organic matter or organic carbon thresholds plus thickness and saturation conditions.

n: Organic soil treatment for converted land (Equation 2.26)
s: In the 2006 Guidelines, land converted to forest, cropland, grassland or settlements on organic soils is treated like the corresponding remaining-land category, with Equation 2.26 for carbon losses.
A family of ISO and GHG Protocol standards for organisation-, project- and product-level GHG and footprint accounting, each with its own edition.

n: Organisation-level versus product-level GHG accounting scope
s: GHG accounting can target the whole organisation (Corporate Standard, ISO 14064) or a single product (PCF/product standards), which differ in boundary and double-counting risk.
Standards that account for aggregate GHG emissions at the company or organisation level, as opposed to product-level footprints.
Approaches for deciding which operations' emissions a company consolidates in its inventory (financial control, equity share, operational control).
Regional default other-cattle data for Tier 1 factors, in 2006 and 2019 editions.
The IPCC 'other halogenated gases' reporting bucket, whose listed compounds differ between the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
IPCC reporting guidance uses 'other halogenated gases' as a catch-all, but the example compounds listed differ between the 2006 reporting-table footnote and the 2019 IPPU text.
IPCC catch-all for fluorinated gases outside the named categories, whose listed compounds differ by edition and reporting context.
The IPCC land-use category covering bare soil, rock, ice and unmanaged land not in the other five categories, as defined in the 2006 and 2019 volumes.

n: Other process uses of carbonates CO2 estimation
s: Tier 1, 2 and 3 methods for CO2 from other process uses of carbonates, differing in the data used to split limestone and dolomite and the calcination fraction.
Overall reduction of an emitted gas as abated fraction times destruction removal efficiency times uptime, at site level or by process type.
Alternative IPCC formulas for recalculating a time-series estimate from overlapping years of an old and a new method.
Ways of building a consistent time series by using the relation between old and new methods or sensors over an overlap period, with two incompatible renderings of Eq. 5.1.
Techniques that link an old and a new series or method using data from an overlap period to build a consistent time series.
Valuation of own-account output as the sum of production costs, with different cost components included in different frameworks.

n: Own-account output valuation at sum of costs
s: Valuation of own-account output as the sum of production costs, with or without a net return to fixed assets depending on producer type.
Variants that attribute investee or project emissions to an investor in proportion to its equity or project-cost share, on a reporting-year or projected-lifetime basis.

IPCC uses 'oxidation factor' for different quantities: the CH4 fraction oxidised in SWDS cover soil, and the carbon fraction oxidised in incineration or open burning. They differ in definition, unit basis and default values.
IPCC term for the fraction oxidised, applied to different quantities (carbon in waste burning or CH4 in landfill cover) in different guidance chapters.
Price and volume indices that use current-period quantities or values as weights.
Indices that use current-period weights (price, volume, spatial and hedonic-imputation forms).

n: PACT PCF biogenic CO2 uptake treatment
s: Two PACT product carbon footprint reporting variants that differ in treating biogenic product CO2 uptake.

Several GHG standards define parameter uncertainty with different scope: input parameters of models, inventory values for a value chain, a single product-life-cycle parameter, or its propagated effect on the total.
GHG Protocol family of definitions of uncertainty about whether input values represent the activity or process being inventoried.
Definitions of parameter uncertainty in the GHG Protocol Corporate, Scope 3 and Product standards, which differ in boundary and in single versus propagated scope.
Alternative PACT conventions for including or excluding biogenic product CO2 uptake in a product carbon footprint.
A family of SNA methods that build stock estimates from past flows, with variants for produced capital, finished-goods inventories and non-renewable resources.

n: Physical allocation of emissions among co-products
s: Allocating an activity's emissions among co-products by a physical factor such as mass, energy or volume.

Allocating the emissions of a multi-output activity according to an underlying physical relationship, defined in the Scope 3 Standard and the Product Standard in different organisational and product contexts.

n: Physical depletion measurement by resource type
s: SEEA-CF rules for recording physical depletion of natural resources, which differ for non-renewable, biological, aquatic and timber resources.
Net physical imports of materials computed as imports minus exports, reported by the same source in two entries.

n: Pool carbon stock change estimation approaches
s: The generic gain-loss and stock-difference approaches for annual carbon stock change in a carbon pool.
Former Tier 1a and 1b schemes for computing potential emissions of fluorinated chemicals, differing in whether product-contained trade is counted.

n: Price and supply adjustment measures (PSAM) definitions
s: Different framings of ETS mechanisms that adjust allowance supply or price in response to market conditions.

ETS design measures that adjust allowance supply or price, defined with different scope across the handbook's passages (high-price injection only, high or low price, or price protection beyond the cap).

n: Price valuation basis of SUT/IO tables
s: Alternative conventions for valuing table entries (basic, producers', purchasers' prices, with margin, tax and f.o.b./c.i.f. treatments).
Different standards define what counts as primary data (value-chain-specific, process-specific, site-specific or emission-factor-based) with non-identical criteria.

n: Primary data definitions across GHG accounting standards
s: Different standards define 'primary data' with slightly different boundaries (value-chain activity, product-life-cycle process, operational-control site/plant).

An indicator of how much of a footprint or inventory rests on primary rather than secondary data, defined differently by PACT (product level, PCF-weighted) and GRI 102 (Scope 3 category level, emissions ratio).
Data-quality indicators reporting how much of a product carbon footprint rests on primary data.
Definitions of process (non-combustion) emissions in the GHG Protocol and IPCC guidance.
Avoiding allocation by dividing common processes into sub-processes that isolate the studied product.
Different formulations of the producer-side carbon responsibility: direct emissions, downstream embodied emissions of primary-input flows, and an α-shared fraction of the sector load.
Different definitions of producer responsibility: direct emissions of a region, or downstream embodied emissions of added-value flows, with α-sharing generalizations.
Definitions of producers' price valuation across the SNA and SUT Handbook, differing in treatment of taxes and subsidies.
Handbook and SNA estimation method using product supply data and fixed ratios to derive use, inventory change, GFCF or quarterly GDP.
Family of national-accounts methods that estimate use-side, inventory, GFCF or quarterly values from product supply data using fixed ratios or residuals.

n: Product (goods and services, national accounts sense)
s: Definitions of a product as a good or service resulting from production, in SNA, SEEA and PACT.
Accounting of GHG emissions at product level (PCF, life cycle inventory, steel product reporting), distinct from region- or nation-level responsibility accounting.
Definitions of which life-cycle processes and emissions belong inside a product-level GHG or carbon footprint boundary.
Descriptions of product life cycle stages in the GHG Protocol Product Standard and the PACT methodology.
IPCC harvested wood product accounting that attributes carbon stock changes to the country of domestic harvest; it is unrelated to carbon responsibility accounting.
Carbon responsibility allocated to the region or nation where emissions physically occur, with variants in how households and exports are treated.
Allocation of emissions to the country or place where they are directly released or produced, differing in wording and in emission or impact scope across sources.

n: Prompt-emission application estimate using a composite emission factor
s: Annual emissions for non-bank applications as net consumption times a composite emission factor (2006 Eq 7.2A and 2019 Eq 7.2a).
Allocation of resource use and impacts to need-satisfaction systems (food, energy, etc.) at the point of final consumption.
Data from a similar activity used as a stand-in for the target activity, with differing statements on whether it may be customized.
Data from a similar activity used as a stand-in for a given activity in GHG Protocol standards, with minor variations in wording.
The price paid by the purchaser to take delivery of a good or service, excluding deductible VAT and including separately paid transport.
Review procedures by personnel not involved in inventory compilation, applied after QC, as defined in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement.
Routine technical activities by compiling personnel to assess and maintain inventory quality, in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and 2019 Refinement.
The symbol R is used for different quantities (root-shoot ratio, recovered CH4) in IPCC chapters; these must not be merged.

n: RAC default charge, lifetime and emission factor ranges
s: Default ranges of charge, lifetime, emission factors and end-of-life parameters for refrigeration and air-conditioning sub-applications, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
IPCC estimation of railway emissions as fuel consumed multiplied by an emission factor and summed over fuel type or locomotive type.
Iterative procedures that adjust a source matrix to control totals, here used for interregional trade flows in input-output tables.

n: Recording convention for goods sent for processing
s: The gross and net principles for recording goods sent for processing, which changed between the 1993 SNA/BPM 5 and the 2008 SNA/BPM 6 versions.
A recovered or flared CH4 quantity subtracted from gross CH4 emissions in IPCC waste equations, with sector-specific definitions, units and indexing.
Methods for allocating recycling process emissions between the life cycle that supplies recovered material and the one that uses recycled material.
Different scoped definitions of recycling: an ISIC/NACE industry-activity definition versus an IPCC waste-stream material-recovery definition.
Two wordings of the reference flow in the GHG Protocol Product Standard: amount of product underlying study results, and amount needed to fulfil the unit-of-analysis function.
The stock of refrigerant or HFC contained in equipment in use, as defined in the IPCC 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
The share of a province's demand for a sector's products that is met by local production, used to regionalise SRIO data.
Growth of an environmental pressure (emissions or resource use) that is lower than growth of an economic or well-being measure.
The principle that a GHG inventory must serve user decision-making needs, stated with corporate wording in the Scope 2 and Scope 3 documents and with product wording in the Product Standard.
Removal of GHGs from the atmosphere by sinks, defined in IPCC glossaries, in the GHG Protocol Product Standard and in the HWP-specific convention.
Income receivable by the owner of a natural resource or non-produced asset for letting another unit use it in production, with scope differing between SEEA 2012 and SNA 2025.
The process of presenting GHG inventory results, defined differently for national inventories (IPCC) and corporate disclosure (GHG Protocol).
The time frame covered by, or at which, emissions information is reported, defined differently by GRI, ETS, GPC, IPCC and the GHG Protocol Scope 3 Standard.

n: Required GHG coverage for product inventories
s: The minimum list of greenhouse gases that must be accounted for in a product carbon footprint, which differs between the GHG Protocol Product Standard and PACT v3.

n: Reservoir CH4 surface-plus-downstream emission by reservoir age
s: Reservoir CH4 emissions computed as surface emissions plus downstream emissions (surface x R_d), with separate equations and emission factors for reservoirs older than, and 20 years old or younger.
Allocation of emissions, activity or value added to the territory or region where the unit is resident rather than where activity physically occurs.
Attributing activities or emissions to the economy of the resident unit rather than the place where they physically occur.
Emission factor for untracked or unclaimed electricity used under the market-based method, with fallback rules when it is unavailable.
Emission factor for untracked or unclaimed electricity or energy used under the market-based method, defined across several GHG Protocol-related sources.
The emission factor or generation mix left after contractual instruments are claimed, used under Scope 2 market-based accounting.
Estimating resource rent as a residual after deducting costs, with different cost and adjustment terms in SEEA 2012 and SNA 2025.
Surplus value from using an asset or natural resource after costs, defined slightly differently in SEEA, SNA and land-income contexts.

n: Resource rent estimation from operating surplus
s: Estimating resource rent as a residual of operating surplus after deducting user costs of produced assets or other costs, with resource-specific variants.
Family of methods estimating resource rent or natural resource value as revenue minus extraction costs, with different starting points and discounting conventions in SEEA and SNA.
Different principles for assigning carbon emission responsibility to producers, consumers, individuals/investors or through product benchmarks.
Different rules for assigning environmental impacts or emissions: to where they physically occur (production), or to where final consumption takes place (consumption/provisioning systems).
The external region outside the accounted system, defined by residency in the SNA and by non-integrated countries in multi-country SUT/IOT tables.
Estimating CH4 from rice fields from daily emission factors, scaling factors, cultivation period and area, with default (Tier 1-style) and country-specific (Tier 2) variants.

n: Road transport CH4 and N2O tiered estimation
s: Tier 1, 2 and 3 methods for road vehicle CH4 and N2O emissions, moving from fuel-based factors to distance-based factors.
Definitions of roundwood in different IPCC editions, differing in volume basis wording.
Emissions in year t from current-year sales times a first-year emission factor plus prior-year sales times its complement, applied to different HFC/PFC applications.

n: Sales-based first-year emission with one-year lag
s: HFC/PFC emissions in year t estimated as a first-year fraction of year-t sales plus the remainder of year t-1 sales, with or without a destruction correction.

n: Sales-year and prior-year F-gas emission formula
s: Emissions equal current-year sales times emission factor plus prior-year sales times one minus emission factor, applied to different F-gas uses.
Statistical formulas for sample uncertainty in the IPCC 2019 uncertainty chapter.
Frameworks that split emissions into direct (scope 1), purchased-energy (scope 2) and other indirect (scope 3) categories, with versions and adaptations for corporate, city and legacy readings.
Definitions of direct (Scope 1) emissions that differ in boundary basis: organizational ownership/control versus city territory.
Direct-emission definitions that differ in boundary: owned or controlled sources (GHG Protocol and GRI) versus sources within a geographic city boundary (GPC).
Direct-emission accounting under one 'Scope 1' label, with the boundary set either by ownership or control (corporate) or by geography (GPC city).
Alternative ways to calculate Scope 2 emissions from purchased electricity: grid-average location-based and instrument/supplier-specific market-based.
Alternative or successive ways to calculate Scope 2 emissions: location-based, market-based, and the earlier Corporate Standard activity-data × emission-factor calculation.

n: Scope 2 calculation method (location-based vs market-based vs EFG)
s: Alternative ways of choosing the electricity emission factor for Scope 2: grid-average location-based, contractual-instrument market-based, and the 2004 standard's EFG rule.
Purchased or grid-supplied energy emission definitions that differ in boundary: energy consumed by the reporting company versus grid-supplied energy used within a city boundary.
Emissions from acquired or grid-supplied electricity, heat, steam and cooling, counted by the consuming company (corporate) or by consumption within a city boundary (GPC).
Indirect emissions from purchased or grid-supplied electricity, steam, heat or cooling, defined for an organizational boundary (GHG Protocol and GRI) or a city boundary (GPC).
Estimating scope 2 emissions from energy use with average emission factors of the grid or location where the energy is consumed, as stated in GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance, GPC and GRI 102.
Definitions of Scope 2 emissions from purchased or grid-supplied energy, bounded by a reporting company or a city.

n: Scope 2 purchased thermal energy emission factor
s: Methods for deriving emission factors for purchased steam, heat or cooling from fuel or electricity inputs and conversion efficiency.
Alternative methods for estimating Scope 3 Category 1 purchased goods and services emissions.
Four alternative ways to estimate upstream cradle-to-gate emissions of purchased goods and services, with increasing reliance on secondary data.
Site-specific and average-data approaches for emissions from processing of sold intermediate products.
Alternative formulas for direct use-phase emissions of sold products, depending on whether the product is a fuel, an energy-consuming product or a GHG-containing product.
Distance-, fuel- and spend-based methods for upstream transportation emissions.
Approaches for screening scope 3 activities or categories and ranking them to decide where to refine data collection.
Different frameworks define Scope 3 (indirect value-chain emissions) with differing boundary basis and reporting requirements.
Different boundary definitions for Scope 3 emissions: city-boundary (GPC) versus organizational value chain (GHG Protocol Corporate/GRI).
Activity-distance × emission-factor calculation used across Scope 3 categories (transport, business travel, commuting) with category-specific activity bases.

n: Scope 3 downstream transport and distribution boundary
s: Scope 3 boundary treatment of transport and distribution of sold products after the point of sale, split between Category 9 and Category 4 by who pays.
Other indirect emissions beyond Scope 2, defined by value-chain position for companies (GHG Protocol) or by out-of-city-boundary location for cities (GPC).

n: Scope 3 emissions definition (corporate vs city boundary)
s: Scope 3 as indirect emissions beyond directly controlled or territorial sources, with the boundary set either by the company value chain or by a city geographic boundary.

n: Scope 3 hybrid method for purchased goods
s: Combining supplier-specific data with secondary data to estimate upstream emissions of purchased goods, with different formulas depending on which supplier data exist.
Frameworks differ on whether Scope 3 reporting is optional, mandatory, or subject to transition relief.
Several standards define secondary data differently, with different boundaries (value chain, product process, company production data, inventory reference source).
Secondary data is defined in several standards by differing criteria (value chain activity, product process, company production data, or inventory purpose).
IPCC definition of fuels manufactured from primary fuels, in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
Secondary production in supply-use and national accounts, viewed as the supply-table off-diagonal or as subsidiary, by-product and joint products.
Distinct meanings of 'sector' across sources: IPCC sectors, SNA institutional sectors, informal-economy sectors, and MRIO industry classes (ISIC and NACE).
Different descriptions and versions of the SEEA Central Framework and its predecessor.
Persons working in unincorporated enterprises they own, whose remuneration is mixed income.
SNA sequence of economic accounts as defined in SNA 2025 and SEEA.

n: Settlements biomass carbon increment estimation (Tier 2 variants)
s: Alternative IPCC Tier 2 ways of estimating annual biomass carbon increment ΔC_G in Settlements Remaining Settlements, based on crown cover area or on individual plants.
Alternative ways of estimating annual carbon accumulation from live biomass increment in Settlements Remaining Settlements.
Default biomass carbon stock before conversion of forest, grassland or cropland to settlements, in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
The IPCC land category for areas that stay in settlement use, as defined in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: Settlements Tier 2b carbon accumulation per tree defaults
s: Default annual carbon accumulation per urban tree by species class, with different species coverage in the 2006 and 2019 versions.
Default IPCC emission factors for SF6 production emissions, selected by whether the major end uses require highly purified gas.
Allocating the emissions of an investee or financed project to an investor by its proportional equity or project-cost share, using either reporting-year emissions or projected lifetime emissions.
Approaches that allocate environmental responsibility between producers and consumers in an input-output framework.
Family of input-output based rules for allocating emissions between producers and consumers, from pure consumption-based footprints to Lenzen-style shared indicators with α/β parameters.
Methods that split emission or material responsibility between producers and consumers rather than assigning it to one side.
Methods that allocate co-responsibility for emissions along supply chains by combining production-based and upstream embodied emissions.
Approaches that distribute responsibility for supply-chain emissions among economic agents rather than assigning it wholly to producers or consumers.
Different ways of splitting responsibility for emissions or impacts between producers, consumers and other agents so that totals are not double-counted.
Approaches that split carbon responsibility between producers, consumers and other actors along the supply chain, using value added or income as the sharing basis.
Different ways of splitting supply-chain emissions or impacts between producers, consumers and other agents, either with fixed coefficients or with shares set by value added.
Methods that allocate co-responsibility for emissions along supply chains, analogous to value added.
Two alternative keys for allocating shared transport emissions to shipments: driven tonne-kilometres or weight times great-circle distance.
Rules fixing which direction of change (emission, removal, gain, loss, credit, penalty) carries a positive or negative sign.
Criteria or rules of thumb used to decide whether a change, category or item is significant enough to be reported, recalculated or treated specially.
An HWP accounting approach that tracks actual carbon fluxes from harvested wood products to the atmosphere and attributes them to the producing or harvesting country.

n: Sinter plant emissions reporting and double-counting rule
s: IPCC rules for reporting sinter plant emissions as IPPU while avoiding double counting of coke fines, in 2006 GL and 2019 Refinement versions.
Definitions of sludge in IPCC Volume 5 that differ in scope between the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.
The monetary amount at which goods, services, labour or assets are exchanged or could be exchanged between independent parties, used as the SNA valuation principle.

n: SOC change worked example: cropland to improved pasture (tropical moist volcanic soil)
s: The IPCC worked example of mineral soil carbon change after cropland converts to improved pasture, given with different default factors and results in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: SOC change worked example: forest to annual cropland (tropical moist volcanic soil)
s: The IPCC Tier 1 worked example of soil organic carbon change after conversion of forest to annual cropland, given with different default factors in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: SOC_REF reference soil organic carbon stock
s: Reference soil organic carbon stock used as the baseline for land-use stock change estimation, with definitions varying by IPCC version and chapter (reference condition, depth, source table).
Different sources define which soil carbon is counted as the soil pool, differing in organic or inorganic carbon, mineral or organic soils, and depth.
Different sources define the soil carbon pool with different boundaries (organic vs inorganic carbon, mineral vs organic soils, depth and size limits).

n: Special purpose entity and unit definitions
s: SNA 2025 uses SPE and special purpose unit/vehicle with different scopes of parent residency and different consolidation treatment.
Rules across standards that give priority to specific, primary or country-specific activity data and emission factors over default or secondary values.
Estimating emissions by multiplying expenditure by an emission intensity per unit of money, with differing factor bases and category scopes.
SNA 2025 allocation of natural resource value between legal owner and extractor.
The SNA 2025 treatment of dividing natural resource value and assets between the legal owner and the extractor, described in several passages.
Accounting approaches that estimate carbon fluxes from changes in carbon stocks, in a general form (PACT) and an HWP-specific form (IPCC).
Annual stock change is estimated as the difference between stock estimates at two times divided by the elapsed years, applied to different pools in the IPCC guidance.

n: Stock-difference method for carbon stock change
s: Annual carbon stock change in a pool is estimated as the difference between stocks at two times divided by the elapsed years, with pool-specific forms (biomass, dead wood and litter, DOM).
Dividing a heterogeneous population, land area or set of emission sources into more homogeneous strata to improve estimation or sampling.

n: Structural decomposition analysis of carbon emissions
s: SDA breaks changes in emissions into driver effects, but the cited studies use different factor sets and system scopes.
Decomposition of changes in regional emissions into driver effects such as intensity, structure, volume and population, with different factor sets for consumption-based and export-embodied emissions.
Different framings of sufficiency as limiting consumption to adequate service levels, in GRO 2024 and AR6 WGIII Chapter 5.
Approaches that take upstream (Scope 3) emissions from supplier-reported data instead of industry averages.
The requirement that total supply of a product equals total use, stated in different price bases, units and scopes across SNA, SEEA and the SUT handbook.
Estimating missing activity data or time-series values from correlated indicator data, in the 2006 and 2019 IPCC guidelines.
Estimating missing emissions or activity data from correlated indicators, either with a regression-based country factor or through time-series splicing.
Variant definitions of sustainable yield in SEEA CF.
Methods for projecting supply and use tables to new macroeconomic totals, namely SUT-RAS and SUT-EURO.

n: SUT projection to new macro totals
s: Methods that project a base-year supply and use table to new macroeconomic totals; the catalog gives SUT-RAS (iterative scaling) and SUT-Euro (growth rates with correction factors) as variants.
Assumptions used to convert supply and use tables into input-output tables: product technology, industry technology and hybrid.
Alternative technology or sales-structure assumptions (models A to D) for deriving symmetric input-output tables from supply and use tables.

n: Symmetry principle in environmental responsibility allocation
s: Requirement that responsibility or pressure be invariant when upstream/downstream or consumption/production roles are interchanged, formulated at flow, agent and indicator level.
Treating a co-product or exported product by subtracting or substituting the emissions of an equivalent product, with scope and applicability differing by source.
Rules on when and how system expansion or substitution credits may be applied to co-products or exported energy in product carbon footprints.
Definitions of systematic and random error in IPCC inventory uncertainty guidance, split by guideline version.
Consumption-based accounting variants that adjust trade-embodied emissions using world-average or technology-corrected emission coefficients instead of the exporter's or importer's own.
Consumption-based accounts that credit or debit countries for the carbon intensity of their exports relative to a world-average coefficient, with formula variants for the treatment of imports.

n: Technology assumptions for product-by-product IOT derivation
s: Alternative assumptions (product, industry, hybrid technology) for converting supply-use tables into product-by-product input-output tables.
Treatment of anticipated asset disposal or closure costs in economic accounts, with different treatments in SNA 2025 and SEEA 2012.
Accounting of emissions, energy or economic activity where they physically occur or are carried out, as opposed to consumption-based or resident-based attribution.
Two perspectives for presenting emissions: by geographic location of release, or by where goods and services are consumed.
Alternative rules for attributing emissions or physical flows to a country or region, either by where they physically occur or by the residence of the producing or consuming unit.
Different conventions for assigning emissions or energy to a region: where activity physically occurs (territory) versus the residence of the actor or consumer.

n: Territory vs residence principle bridging in energy-extended MRIO
s: The mismatch between territory-based energy data and residence-based monetary MRIO tables, and the procedure to reconcile them.
Assurance by persons from an organization independent of the inventory determination process, defined in the GHG Protocol standards for scope 3, general GHG and product inventories.

n: Tier 1 abandoned underground mine methane estimation
s: Tier 1 estimation of methane from abandoned underground coal mines, with different equation forms in the 2006 Guidelines and the 2019 Refinement.

n: Tier 1 biomass carbon change on land-use conversion
s: Per-hectare biomass carbon stock change from conversion to a new land use as before-minus-after stocks plus growth, applied separately for each destination land use.

n: Tier 1 coal-mine emission = EF x production x conversion factor
s: Tier 1 coal-mine gas emissions as emission factor times coal production times a volume-to-mass conversion factor, by mine type, gas and guideline version.

n: Tier 1 DOM carbon stock change on converted land
s: Tier 1 dead organic matter carbon change on converted land based on stock difference times converted area, with land-category-specific assumptions on the transition period.

n: Tier 1 drained organic soil CO2 emission (area x EF)
s: CO2 loss from drained organic soils as drained area times a climate-specific emission factor, summed over climate zones.
IPCC Tier 1 CO2 loss from drained organic soils as the sum over climate zones of area × annual emission factor, applied to forest land and cropland.
Tier 1 default-factor estimation of fluorinated-compound and GHG emissions from electronics manufacturing using a capacity-based (2006) or production-based (2019) activity basis.
The IPCC Tier 1 default-EF estimation of electronics manufacturing emissions, in a capacity-based (2006) and a substrate-production-based (2019) form.

n: Tier 1 enteric fermentation CH4 inventory method (versioned)
s: Tier 1 enteric methane as default emission factor times livestock population summed over categories, with differing scaling-factor records between the 2006 and 2019 sources.

n: Tier 1 fixed default set and no-mixing rule
s: Rules that Tier 1 default factor sets and gas sets must not be modified or mixed with higher-tier estimates, with sector-specific variations in wording and exceptions.
Tier 1 fugitive GHG emissions at gasification stations as feedstock or syngas energy content times an emission factor, converted from kg to Gg.

n: Tier 1 gasification fugitive emission equation (FS x EF x 10^-6)
s: Fugitive GHG from gasification stations estimated as feedstock or syngas energy (TJ) times a kg/TJ EF, converted to Gg, for different facility types.

s: Activity data is a quantitative measure of a level of activity that results in GHG emissions over a given period.

loc.section: For most emission sources, cities will need to estimate GHG emissions by multiplying activity data by an emission factor associated with the activity being measured. Activity data is a quantitative measure of a level of activity that results in GHG emissions taking place during a given period of time (e.g., volume of gas used, kilometers driven, tonnes of waste sent to landfill, etc.). An emission factor is a measure of the mass of GHG emissions relative to a unit of activity. For example, estimating CO_2 emissions from the use of electricity involves multiplying data on kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity used by the emission factor (kgCO_2 /kWh) for electricity, which will depend on the technology and type of fuel used to generate the electricity. s: In the GPC, 'city' refers to any geographically discernible subnational entity, such as a community, town, city or province.

loc.section: The GPC requires cities to measure and disclose a comprehensive GHG inventory using two distinct but complementary approaches. One captures emissions from both production and consumption activities taking place within the city boundary, including some emissions released outside the city boundary. The other categorizes all emissions into “scopes,” depending on where they physically occur. Separate accounting of emissions physically released within the city boundary should be used for aggregation of multiple city inventories in order to avoid double counting. The GPC is divided into three main parts: • Part I introduces the GPC reporting and accounting principles, sets out how to define the inventory boundary, specifies reporting requirements and offers a sample reporting template • Part II provides overarching and sector-specific accounting and reporting guidance for sourcing data and calculating emissions, including calculation methods and equations • Part III shows how inventories can be used to set mitigation goals and track performance over time, and shows how cities can manage inventory quality Note, the term “city” is used throughout this document to refer to any geographically discernable subnational entity, such as a community, town, city, or province, and covers all levels of subnational jurisdiction as well as local government as legal entities of public administration.

s: The GPC inventory boundary identifies the geographic area, time span, gases and emission sources covered by a city GHG inventory.

loc.section: To use the GPC, cities must first define an inventory boundary. This identifies the geographic area, time span, gases, and emission sources, covered by a GHG inventory. Any geographic boundary may be used for the GHG inventory. Depending on the purpose of the inventory, the boundary can align with the administrative boundary of a local government, a ward or borough within a city, a combination of administrative divisions, a metropolitan area, or another geographically identifiable entity. The GPC is designed to account for GHG emissions in a single reporting year and covers the seven gases covered by the Kyoto Protocol (Section 3.3 in the report).

s: A unit that expresses GHG emissions from different gases using global warming potential.

loc.section: The International System of Units (SI units) should be used for measurement and reporting of activity data, and all GHG emissions data shall be reported as metric tonnes of each GHG as indicated in Table 4.3, as well as CO_2 equivalents (CO_2 e). The same applies where emission factors or emissions data are unavailable for specific gases. CO_2 e is a universal unit of measurement that accounts for the global warming potential (GWP) when measuring and comparing GHG emissions from different gases. The time period generally used for GWP is 100 years. There are also 20-year GWPs that are available. It is used to evaluate the climate impact of releasing (or avoiding releasing) different greenhouse gases on a common basis.

s: CHP is simultaneous generation of electricity and useful heat, and CCHP adds cooling, typically in district energy systems.

loc.section: Cogeneration, or combined heat and power (CHP), is the use of power plant or heat engine systems to simultaneously generate electricity and useful heat. Tri-generation, or combined cooling, heat and power (CCHP), refers to the simultaneous generation of electricity, heat, and cooling. GHG emissions from these facilities should be calculated based on the quantity of fuel combusted. These facilities are generally called district energy systems. Such systems provide energy to multiple consumers, though they often have only one generation facility and serve a more limited geographic area than electricity grids. Emissions from this combustion shall be reported in scope 1 for grid- • supplied energy production (1.4.4), and for added transparency, cities can identify the portion of those scope 1 (territorial) emissions attributable to cooling or heat/steam vs. Electricity production.^29 This allocation can be performed using the percentage of each energy output (% of total MMBUT or GJ from electricity and from heat). It is important to distinguish the cogeneration plants or district energy systems from the autoproducers (which generate electricity/heat wholly or partly for their own use, and is an activity that supports their primary activity) that maybe used in residential, commercial or industrial buildings. In these cases, the energy is not being sent to the grid and therefore cannot be included in I.4.4 and should instead be included in the relevant scope 1 emissions (I.1, I.2 or I.3). loc.section: The updated Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Inventories (GPC) offers cities and local governments a robust, transparent, and globally accepted framework to consistently identify, calculate, and report on city greenhouse gas emissions. This includes emissions released within city boundaries as well as those occurring outside them as a result of city activities. The GPC establishes credible emissions accounting and reporting practices that help cities develop an emissions baseline, set mitigation goals, create more targeted climate action plans, and track progress over time, as well as strengthen opportunities for cities to partner with other levels of government and increase access to local and international climate financing. It has been revised to align with the 2019 Refinement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories, to clarify ambiguities, and to provide further methodological guidance. Since its launch in 2014, the GPC has been used by cities across the world to calculate and report emissions, and has enabled decision makers to inform national and sub- national policy based on the best available science. Over 50% of the cities reporting to CDP in 2020 noted that they used GPC or another methodology closely aligned with it to develop their inventories. This globally recognized framework has been adopted as a central component of international reporting platforms like the CDP-ICLEI Unified Reporting Platform and initiatives such as the Global Covenant of Mayors (a merger of the Compact of Mayors and EU Covenant of Mayors). Urban areas are a logical setting for implementing and measuring climate action. Local governments can be more nimble where regional or national governments are often more restricted by bureaucracy. Mayors, local councils, and community leaders understand local needs and constraints, which often results in bolder, more effective actions. Local governments can track the performance of city services, guide change in the community, and set regulations that govern land use, building efficiency, and local transportation. Thousands of cities are taking action to reduce emissions and improve climate resilience, including during the COVID-19 pandemic, which has propelled cities to reimagine how they operate. The revised GPC provides these cities and their advocates with a global standard to track greenhouse gas reductions and lead the way to a more sustainable future.

loc.section: C40 helps cities identify, develop, and implement local policies and programs that have collective global impact. Working across multiple sectors and initiative areas, C40 convenes networks of cities with common goals and challenges, providing a suite of services in support of their efforts: direct technical assistance; facilitation of peer-to- peer exchange; and research, knowledge management & communications. C40 is also positioning cities as a leading force for climate action around the world, defining and amplifying their call to national governments for greater support and autonomy in creating a sustainable future.

s: HWP are all wood material leaving harvest sites that constitutes a carbon reservoir, with holding time varying by product use.

loc.section: Harvested wood products (HWP) include all wood material that leaves harvest sites and constitutes a carbon reservoir (the time carbon is held in products will vary depending on the product and its uses). Fuel wood, for example, may be burned in the year of harvest, and many types of paper are likely to have a use life less than five years, including recycling. Wood used for panels in buildings, however, may be held for decades to over 100 years. Discarded HWP can be deposited in solid waste disposal sites where they may subsist for long periods of time. Due to this storage in products in use and in SWDS, the oxidation of HWP in a given year could be less, or potentially more, than the total amount of wood harvested in that year.

s: An emission factor that considers emissions at every stage of a material or fuel's life, unlike activity-based factors.

loc.section: Emission factors convert activity data into a mass of GHG emissions; tonnes of CO_2 released per kilometer travelled, for example, or the ratio of CH_4 emissions produced to amount of waste landfilled. Emission factors should be relevant to the inventory boundary, specific to the activity being measured, and sourced from credible government, industry, or academic sources. Emission factors may be activity-based, or life-cycle based. Activity-based emission factors include emissions at the point of the final activity (e.g. combustion of fuel). Life-cycle emission factors, on the other hand, consider emissions at every stage of a material/ fuel’s life (e.g. extraction, processing, transport, combustion). Activity-based emission factors must be used in order to comply with the GPC (in particular, its differentiation between scopes). More information on life-cycle emission factors can be found in the Technical Guidance for Calculating Scope 3 Emissions .

s: An LGO inventory measures emissions from a local government's own municipal operations and is not a GPC requirement, though its data may inform the city-wide inventory.

loc.section: In addition to compiling a city-wide GHG inventory, local governments may also want to measure GHG emissions from their own municipal operations via a local government operations (LGO) inventory. An LGO inventory allows local governments to identify GHG reduction opportunities across their jurisdiction and demonstrate leadership in taking action. While this is not a requirement of the GPC, LGO data may also be useful in compiling information for a city-wide inventory. For example, activity data from city-owned or operated buildings, facilities, landfills or land can be more precise than estimating activity data from those sectors based on scaled regional or national data. Appendix B provides further information on developing an LGO inventory.

loc.section: The city-induced framework gives cities the option of selecting between two reporting levels: BASIC or BASIC+. The BASIC level covers scope 1 and scope 2 emissions from stationary energy and transportation, as well as scope 1 and scope 3 emissions from waste. BASIC+ involves additional data collection and calculation processes, requiring emissions from IPPU, emissions and removals from AFOLU, and emissions from transboundary transportation. loc.section: • CRF uses the BASIC approach but does not use the specific terminology. It requires cities to report on emissions from stationary energy, in-boundary transportation and in-boundary waste, and encourages reporting on energy generation, IPPU and AFOLU wherever relevant. • IEAP requires two levels of reporting: city-wide emissions, and emissions from the operations of local government; • ISDGC requires that upstream GHG emissions embedded in food, water, fuel and building materials consumed in cities be reported as additional information items. It recommends cities or urban regions with populations over 1 million persons to use its reporting standard, and cities with populations below 1 million may use less detailed reporting tables such as BEI/MEI; • BEI/MEI only requires mandatory quantification of CO_2 emissions due to final energy consumption. Reporting of emissions from non-energy sectors and non- CO_2 emissions are not mandatory. It was specifically designed for the signatory cities participating in the EU Covenant of Mayors Initiative to track their progress toward the goal set under the initiative, and therefore doesn’t cover interactions with other policies, such as EU ETS, in its framework; • U.S. Community Protocol introduces the concepts of “sources” and “activities” rather than the scopes framework, where “sources” is equivalent to scope 1, and “activities” is equivalent to 2 and 3, with some overlap in scope 1. Activities are recognized as those processes which can be managed for emissions reductions regardless of where the emissions occur. The U.S. Community Protocol uses different emission categories than IPCC Guidelines and also provides a reporting framework with Five Basic Emissions Generating Activities and some additional and voluntary reporting frameworks (see table A.2); • PAS 2070 provides two methodologies to assess city GHG emissions. These recognize cities as both consumers and producers of goods and services. The direct plus supply chain (DPSC) methodology captures territorial GHG emissions and those associated with the largest supply chains serving cities and is consistent with the GPC. The consumption-based (CB) methodology uses input-output modeling to estimate direct and life cycle GHG emissions for all goods and services consumed by residents of a city. Some other important features, including primary audience, use of the “scopes” framework, inclusion of transboundary emissions and emission sources categories are also compared and summarized below. Primary audience The standards reviewed are developed for accounting and reporting of city-level, national-level and corporate or organizational-level inventories. Most of the standards were developed for global use, while two standards were designed to target specific groups. The BEI/ MEI was designed for EU cities that participated in the Covenant of Mayors Initiative to track their progress to achieve their SEAP goal. The U.S. Community Protocol was designed as a management framework to guide U.S. local governments to account for and report their GHG emissions associated with the communities they represent, with an emphasis on sources and activities over which U.S. local governments have the authority to influence. Adoption of “scopes” framework and inclusion of transboundary emissions All standards reviewed adopt the scopes framework except for the U.S. Community Protocol, which includes two central categories of emissions: 1) GHG emissions that are produced by community-based “sources” located within the community boundary, and 2) GHG emissions produced as a consequence of community “activities”. To better illustrate these two concepts using the scopes framework, emissions from sources refer to scope 1 (territorial) emissions, emissions from activities refer to processes that take place within the community boundary which result in transboundary emissions. All standards cover both in-boundary and transboundary emissions, except for the BEI/MEI method, which only considers scope 1 (territorial) and scope 2 emissions. Emission source categories 2006 IPCC Guidelines divide emissions sources into four sectors: Energy, IPPU, Waste and AFOLU . All other reviewed standards generally followed this division

n: Aviation LTO and cruise allocation completeness
