s: When data collection, methods or models are revised, good practice is to recalculate the complete time series, using proxy data or extrapolation where needed.

n: Top-down and bottom-up matching for CO2 and CH4/N2O
s: For CO2, fuel-statistics and VKT-based estimates should be compared and anomalies explained; for CH4 and N2O, good practice is to ensure top-down and bottom-up approaches match and document deviations.

loc.section: Comparison of emissions using alternative approaches

n: Top-down fuel use uncertainty and CO2 method choice for railways
s: Top-down fuel use uncertainty is about 5 percent, bottom-up disaggregated data are at least 10 percent uncertain, and the guidance suggests top-down CO2 with bottom-up CO2 used for QA/QC.

n: Transport sector boundary: international bunkers excluded from totals
s: Fuel sold to air or marine vessels engaged in international transport should, as far as possible, be excluded from transport totals and reported separately.

n: Vehicle classification for CH4 and N2O Tier 2 and 3
s: Vehicle type should follow reporting classification 1.A.3.b and be split by age and, where possible, fuel sulphur content, as CH4 may otherwise be underestimated.

n: Water-borne navigation domestic/international fuel split by flag or nationality
s: Domestic and international water-borne navigation definitions are independent of the carrier's nationality or flag.

n: Accounting of drained methane for Tier 1 and Tier 2
s: For Tiers 1 and 2, drained methane that is vented should not be re-counted, while drained methane that is flared or utilised should be subtracted.
Losses from CO2 capture are assigned to the industry where capture occurs, while transport, injection and storage losses are assessed in Chapter 5.

n: CO2 capture, transport, injection and storage boundary for fugitive CO2
s: Fugitive CO2 from capture is accounted for in the industry where capture occurs, while fugitive CO2 from transport, injection and storage is accounted for in category 1.C.

n: CO2 factor boundary (direct CO2 only, except flaring)
s: CO2 factors cover direct CO2 emissions only, except for flaring factors, which include indirect CO2 from atmospheric oxidation of non-CO2 carbon emissions.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories 4.52

n: CO2 from hydrogen production and sweetening: category assignment
s: Formation CO2 released from gas sweetening is reported under 1.B.2.b.i, and CO2 from hydrogen production at refineries and upgraders under 1.B.2.a.i, with a warning against also reporting the feedstock as fuel.
Detailed sector or subcategory methodology manuals must conform to the common IPCC framework so emission results are comparable across countries.

n: Each mine counted once in the active-to-abandoned transition
s: When a mine moves from active to abandoned status, it must be included once and only once in the national inventory.

n: Emission factor selection and activity data basis
s: Selected emission factors must be valid for the application and expressed on the same basis as the activity data, and may need correction for site, regional and operating differences.

loc.section: 2004 The API Compendium is available at:

s: Equation 4.1.2 is for Tier 1 and Tier 2 only and is not appropriate for Tier 3 methods, which use mine-specific drained and recovered methane.

loc.section: ADJUSTMENT FOR METHANE UTILISATION OR FLARING

n: Flooded abandoned mines may be assigned zero emissions
s: Mines known to be completely flooded may be assigned an emissions value of zero.

n: Fully flooded abandoned mines assigned zero emissions
s: Fully flooded mines should be kept in inventory databases but assigned zero emissions.

n: Inventory year for coal seam degasification emissions
s: The source requires degasification-related methane emissions and recovery to be accounted in the inventory year in which the operations occur rather than the year the seam is mined through.

n: Inventory year timing for abandoned mine methane
s: Abandoned mine methane emissions are to be accounted for in the inventory year in which the emissions and recovery operations occur.

loc.section: EMISSIONS REDUCTIONS FROM METHANE RECOVERY AT ABANDONED MINES

n: Missing inventory years for surface mine emissions
s: For missing surface mine inventory years, emissions may be scaled to production only when the number of active mines has not changed significantly.

n: NMVOC derivation from methane for selected sources
s: For selected sources NMVOC factors are derived from methane factors using stated NMVOC-to-CH4 mass ratios.
Changes in results between inventory recalculations must be discussed, and changes due strictly to methods and factors should be highlighted.

n: Recovered and flared methane is subtracted from abandoned mine emissions
s: Methane reductions from recovery and utilisation or flaring projects at abandoned mines are subtracted from the emissions estimate.

n: Recovered methane subtraction for abandoned mines without Tier 3
s: Without a Tier 3 method, total recovered and utilised methane is subtracted from total abandoned mine emissions, with the result not below zero.

loc.section: Emissions Reductions through Recovery and Utilization

n: Reporting of fuel use for venting and flaring
s: Emissions from fuel gas used for purge, blanket, supply or flare-enrichment purposes must be reported under venting or flaring subcategories rather than under Category 1.A.

n: Reporting transparency requirement for oil and gas fugitive emission inventories
s: Inventory reports should include method summaries and source data references so that reported emissions can be retraced.
Each closed or abandoned mine must be classified in one and only one inventory database.

n: Table 4.2.1 IPCC sector split for oil and natural gas (1.B.2)
s: Table 4.2.1 gives the IPCC category codes 1.B.2 for oil and natural gas, with subcategories for oil and natural gas and their venting, flaring, all-other, and sub-activity classes.
Table 4.2.4 factors apply only to systems built and operated to North American and Western European standards.

n: Table 4.2.4 factors are examples under stated industry practices
s: Table 4.2.4 factors are presented as examples and reflect a listed set of mature, regulated, well-maintained industry practices.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories 4.62

n: Table 4.2.6 Typical activity data requirements by assessment tier
s: Table 4.2.6 lists minimum required activity data for each assessment tier and primary source category of oil and gas fugitive emissions.

n: Table 4.2.7 Tier 1 activity data values and guidance
s: Table 4.2.7 gives the Tier 1 activity data value, its unit, and guidance for obtaining each value by oil and gas category.

n: Table 4.2.8 Classification of gas losses as low, medium or high
s: Table 4.2.8 gives indicative low, medium and high yearly emission factors for natural gas facilities, used to qualify specific methane losses for reasonableness.
Tier 1 emission factors are expressed per unit of oil or gas throughput.

n: Tier 1 gassy-mine percentage default values by abandonment interval
s: Tier 1 default gassy-mine percentages range from 0 to 10 percent for 1900-1925 and up to 100 percent for later intervals.

loc.section: Tier 1: Global Average Approach – Abandoned Underground Mines

n: Tier 1 post-mining CH4 emission factor values
s: The source gives low, average and high Tier 1 post-mining CH4 emission factors.

n: Tier 1 post-mining emission factor values for surface mines
s: Post-mining Tier 1 factors for surface mines are 0, 0.1 and 0.2 m^3 per tonne, with the average used unless country-specific evidence supports another value.

n: Tier 1 surface mining CH4 emission factor values and selection rule
s: Tier 1 surface mining factors are 0.3, 1.2 and 2.0 m^3 per tonne, with low or high values selected by overburden depth.

n: Tier 1 underground mining CH4 emission factor values by depth
s: The source gives low, average and high Tier 1 underground mining CH4 emission factors and says the low end applies to mining depths under 200 m and the high value to depths over 400 m.
The Tier 1 approach should only be used for non-key sources.

n: Tier 2 decline coefficients a and b by coal rank (Table 4.1.9)
s: Default Tier 2 decline coefficients a and b are given for anthracite, bituminous and sub-bituminous coal, to be used only when country or basin data are unavailable.

n: Tier 2 default active mine emission rate range (Table 4.1.8)
s: Default active mine emissions prior to abandonment are given as low 1.3 and high 38.8 million m3 per year, for use when country or basin data are not available.
New Tier 2 factors reflect real industry changes and must not be applied to earlier years in the time series.
Where Tier 3 approaches are used, their procedures must be detailed or cited because the IPCC Guidelines do not describe a standard Tier 3 approach for the oil and gas sector.

n: Tier 3 not feasible for post-mining emissions
s: The source states that direct measurement of post-mining emissions is not feasible, so Tier 1 or Tier 2 emission factor approaches are used.

n: Tier 3 reuse rule for Tier 2 emission factors
s: Where a Tier 3 approach in one year yields Tier 2 emission factors for other years, those other years are reported as Tier 2.

n: Tier selection decision tree for oil and natural gas fugitive emissions
s: Decision trees are applied successively to each subcategory, starting from data availability for Tier 3, then Tier 2, then key-category significance, with Tier 1 as the fallback.

n: Trend analysis and uncertainty reporting requirement
s: Reported results should include trend analysis of emissions, activity data and intensities, and state expected accuracy and main uncertainty areas.
When the alternative Tier 2 approach is used, reported venting or flaring data for the same sources must not also be counted.

n: Accounting pathways for geological storage emissions
s: Only CO2 leakage to the ground surface or seabed from the geological storage reservoir needs to be considered in accounting.

n: Boundary between EOR surface and subsurface emission categories
s: Fugitive emissions from EOR/EGR/ECBM surface facilities belong to oil and gas operations, while underground reservoir emissions belong to geological storage sites.

n: Capture reporting linked to long-term storage
s: CO2 capture should not be reported unless it is linked to long-term storage, and captured mass must not exceed stored mass plus reported fugitive emissions.

loc.section: QA/QC for the whole CCS system

n: CCGS scope of emission estimation guidance
s: The chapter provides emission estimation guidance only for CO2 transport, injection and geological storage, not for other storage options or for capture and compression.
In these Guidelines the capture systems boundary includes compression and any dehydration or conditioning before transport.

n: CO2 capture technology pathway guidance references
s: Emission estimation guidance for CO2 capture and compression is located in other volumes depending on the CO2 source.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories 5.7

s: All CO2 and, where relevant, CH4 emissions from all CO2 storage sites should be included in the national inventory.
Any emissions from compression of CO2 at the storage site should be measured and reported when arriving CO2 pressure is below injection pressure.
The capture country reports captured, transported and exported CO2, while the importing country reports imports, transport emissions and storage-site emissions.

n: Energy use from capture, compression, transport and injection reporting rule
s: Emissions from fossil fuels used for capture, compression, transport and injection are reported in the energy use categories, not in this chapter.
Geological storage may occur onshore or offshore in deep saline formations, depleted oil or gas fields, and coal seams, with or without enhanced recovery operations.
The injection system runs from the end of the transport pipeline or ship offloading facility to the geological storage reservoir and includes surface facilities and injection wells.
Fugitive emissions from a tank-type CO2 buffer are reported under transport category 1C1 c, while a geological buffer follows geological storage treatment and is reported under 1C3.

loc.section: 5.4.3 Intermediate storage facilities on CO_2 transport routes

n: Leakage to seabed treated as atmospheric emissions
s: For offshore geological storage, leakage to the seabed should be considered as emissions to the atmosphere for inventory compilation.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories 5.15

n: Monitoring plan requirements for storage sites
s: Each storage site's monitoring plan should cover background fluxes, injected mass, injection system emissions, surface or seabed fluxes, post-injection monitoring, and periodic verification of emission estimates.

n: No double accounting of CO2 storage across countries
s: When capture and storage occur in different countries, the national inventory compilers must arrange to avoid double counting of storage.
Emissions must be recalculated when monitoring detection improves, previously unrecorded emissions are identified, or updated models and monitoring corroborate them.

If an appropriate governing body regulates CO2 capture and storage, the inventory compiler may use its emissions information, with supporting documentation showing consistency with IPCC practice; otherwise the Tier 3 methodology is followed.

n: Ship transport fugitive emission factors not available
s: Default emission factors for fugitive emissions from CO2 transport by ship are not available, so losses should be metered and reported.
Emissions from CO2 transport, injection and storage are reported under category 1C, while capture emissions are reported under the IPCC sector where capture takes place.

n: Specific mass of methane for pipeline factor conversion
s: Natural gas leakage factors in m3 are converted to mass using 0.7 kg/m3 for methane.
Tier 1 pipeline emission factors are given per gas throughput, and pipeline length is used for CCS-specific facility-based estimation.
The transport system starts at the outlet of the compression/conditioning plant and ends at the downstream end of a pipeline or ship offloading facility.
Confidence intervals or probability curves may be used for CCS uncertainty when percentage uncertainties are not applicable.
The amount of CO2 injected through a well can be monitored by equipment at the wellhead, and reporting injected mass from direct measurement is good practice where no default method is suggested.

n: Activity data for excluded carbon flows (Table 6.2)
s: Table 6.2 specifies which activity data (deliveries or total deliveries) must be used for each fuel whose carbon is excluded from fuel combustion emissions in the Reference Approach.
Bitumen deliveries give no fuel combustion emissions in the inventory year, and white spirit is excluded as solvent emissions.

n: Carbon conservation assumption in Reference Approach
s: The Reference Approach assumes carbon is conserved across the energy supply chain, so carbon in crude oil equals total carbon in its derived products.

n: Coke delivered to iron, steel and non-ferrous industries excluded
s: Coke delivered for iron and steel and non-ferrous metals industries should be excluded from total carbon.

loc.section: COKE OVEN COKE AND PETROLEUM COKE

s: Default carbon content applies only when country-specific values are unavailable; country-specific values should be weighted averages of detailed consumption values.

n: Energy conversion on net calorific value basis
s: Apparent consumption should be converted to terajoules on a net calorific value basis, with gross values allowed only where the detailed inventory used them.
Table 6.1 lists the main products whose carbon is excluded as feedstock, reductant or non-energy product.

n: Feedstock carbon fully excluded in Reference Approach
s: In the Reference Approach all carbon in fuel delivered as feedstock is excluded, even where part is used for heat raising, to keep the method simple.
All deliveries of lubricating oil are excluded from the Reference Approach.

n: Net deliveries for petrochemical feedstock activity data
s: For the Reference Approach, deliveries used as activity data should be net of oils returned to refineries from petrochemical processing.
All quantities of paraffin waxes are excluded from the Reference Approach.

n: Secondary fuel production excluded from apparent consumption
s: Production or manufacture of secondary fuels must be ignored in the apparent consumption calculation because their carbon is already in primary fuel supply.
An increase in stocks is a positive stock change that is subtracted from supply, and a stock reduction increases apparent consumption.

n: Uncertainty analysis when Reference Approach is primary
s: If the Reference Approach is the primary accounting method for CO2 from fuel combustion, good practice requires an uncertainty analysis.

n: Biomass CO2 double-counting rule in fuel combustion worksheets
s: Emissions from combustion of biofuels are reported as information items and excluded from sectoral and national totals to avoid double counting.

n: Fuel combustion source category mapping for worksheets
s: Each fuel combustion worksheet should be copied for each source category listed in Table 2.16 of the Stationary Combustion chapter, with the source category name inserted next to the worksheet number.

n: Fuel consumption inclusion rules for Tier 1 worksheets
s: Column A of the fuel combustion worksheets should include only fuel consumed as fuel, excluding feedstock, petrochemical feedstock and waste burned without recovery, with fuel-specific exceptions.

n: Reference Approach CO2 conversion to molecular weight ratio
s: The Reference Approach converts net carbon in Gg C to Gg CO2 using the factor 44/12.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.14

n: Allocation rule for CO2 from fuel combustion vs. industrial process (Box 1.1)
s: Combustion emissions from fuels derived from an IPPU feedstock are normally allocated to the IPPU source category where the process occurs, unless the derived fuels are transferred for combustion in another category.

n: Asphalt, road paving and roofing emissions reporting
s: Emissions from asphalt production, road paving and roofing are reported under 2D4, and bitumen or road oil used in this activity does not result in CO2 emissions.

n: Attribution of indirect N2O to original nitrogen source
s: Indirect N2O from IPPU nitrogen deposition is attributed to the original source of the nitrogen, which is an accounting convention for consistency.
The CO2 completeness check excludes waste incineration, flaring, venting and fugitive Category 1B emissions.

Tier 1 methods are not appropriate for tracking capture; capture should be an additional term, and good practice is to deduct captured CO2 in higher-tier calculations rather than modify emission factors.

n: Default assumption on CO2 capture and storage in IPPU
s: The default assumption is that no carbon dioxide capture and storage takes place.

n: Double counting avoidance for non-energy use
s: Compilers must understand the non-energy use definition used in their country to prevent double counting and ensure CO2 emissions are not overlooked.

loc.section: 1 Total hydrocarbon input into the process 2 Part of the input allocated to final energy use in energy statistics 3 Part of the input allocated to feedstock / non-energy use in energy statistics 4 Part of the input allocated to energy conversions in energy statistics 5 By-products used as fuels within the process 6 By-products used as fuels within the source category to which the process belongs 7 By products exported to other source categories 8 Main products 9 Emissions

n: Double-counting rule for captured CO2 split between combustion and process categories
s: When combustion and process emissions from captured CO2 are reported separately, the same CO2 must not be double counted, preferably allocating captured total in proportion to CO2 generated in each category.

n: Emissions from petrochemical feedstock uses allocated to 2B8
s: Emissions from feedstock uses in the petrochemical industry should be addressed under 2B8 Petrochemical and Carbon Black Production.

n: Feedstock balance check 10 percent investigation threshold
s: Differences between feedstock supply and requirements exceeding 10 percent of supply should trigger data checks and investigation.

loc.section: Step 3: Actions arising from the comparison

n: Feedstock balance check direction of discrepancy interpretation
s: When feedstock supply exceeds requirements it may indicate omitted processes; when requirements exceed supply it may indicate fuels reported elsewhere, net-versus-gross definition issues, or overstated requirements.

loc.section: Step 3: Actions arising from the comparison

n: Good-practice choice between mass-balance and emission-factor approaches
s: Mass-balance is good practice over emission-factor when accurate activity data are available and its drawbacks do not apply; the emission-factor approach is preferred under the drawback conditions.

loc.section: 1.5.2 Strengths and weaknesses of the mass-balance approach

n: Industrial process gas notation key (X and asterisk) in Table 1.1
s: In Table 1.1, X marks gases for which methodological guidance is provided in the volume and asterisk marks gases whose emissions may occur without guidance.

n: Mineral turpentine and solvent CO2 reporting
s: Solvent-use CO2 from mineral turpentine and coal-derived aromatic solvents is reported in IPPU category 2D3 as stated in the footnotes.
Monetary production values reflect both quantity and price, so they fluctuate with prices and should be used with care.

n: Off-site combustion of off-gases accounted as Energy sector fuel combustion
s: Off-gases combusted off-site in a different sector are accounted separately as fuel combustion in the Energy Sector.

n: Post-consumer waste exclusion from IPPU sector
s: Emissions from subsequent uses of used non-energy products are excluded from the IPPU volume and are covered under Energy or Waste Sectors.
CO2 from fuel consumed by refineries for manufacturing activities, including basic chemicals for sale, is reported as Energy Sector emissions.

n: Reporting of CO2 from blast furnace gas and chemical off-gases in Energy sector
s: CO2 from blast furnace gas and chemical off-gases is reported in the Energy sector only when utilised in public power or heat production.
All emissions from the production of synthesis gas are reported in the IPPU Sector under the allocation principle in Box 1.1.

loc.section: 1 Total hydrocarbon input into the process 2 Part of the input allocated to final energy use in energy statistics 3 Part of the input allocated to feedstock / non-energy use in energy statistics 4 Part of the input allocated to energy conversions in energy statistics 5 By-products used as fuels within the process 6 By-products used as fuels within the source category to which the process belongs 7 By products exported to other source categories 8 Main products 9 Emissions

n: Table 1.4 fossil fuels usable as chemical feedstock or reductant
s: Table 1.4 lists fossil fuels that can be used as chemical feedstock or reductant, by solids, liquids, gases and other fuels.

n: Waste gas and product-carbon allocation between IPPU and Energy sectors
s: Some product-carbon emissions are reported in Waste or Energy Sectors, and CO2 from non-energy use may be included in Energy Sector 1A where IPPU waste gases are used and reported there.
In absence of actual data, good practice assumes calcination of 100 percent or very close; for LKD, F_d of 1.00 zeroes the LKD correction.

n: Carbonate CO2 emission factors and formula weights (Table 2.1)
s: Table 2.1 gives formula weights and CO2 emission factors per tonne of carbonate for common carbonate species, with a rounding rule for final results.
Carbonate consumption is assumed equal to raw material mined plus imported minus exported.

n: Carbonate inputs for glass: primary vs carbonated hydroxide
s: Mined carbonate glass raw materials produce primary CO2 and should be included, while carbonates produced by carbonation of a hydroxide should not be included.

n: CKD correction in Tier 3 is subtractive
s: Under Tier 3, emissions attributed to uncalcined CKD not recycled to the kiln are subtracted, unlike Tier 2 where they are added.

n: CKD emissions equal to 2 percent assumption must be reported
s: If the assumption that CKD emissions equal 2 percent of clinker process emissions is used, it must be transparently reported.

n: Clay consumption default loss factor for ceramics Tier 1
s: For Tier 1 ceramics clay consumption, clay is estimated by multiplying production by a default loss factor of 1.1.

n: Clinker trade correction and cement-process completeness rule
s: Tier 1 requires net clinker import/export correction, Tier 3 requires all clinker-producing plants and all carbonate inputs, and cement process emissions must avoid double counting with other source categories and energy.

n: Default assumption of no CO2 capture
s: The default assumption is that no CO2 capture and storage occurs, and captured CO2 must not be double-counted between energy and IPPU categories.

n: Default limestone/dolomite allocation for Tier 1 and Tier 2
s: Where the carbonate breakdown for an industry is unknown, a default allocation of 85 percent limestone and 15 percent dolomite is used and must be documented.

n: Direct cement-based emission factor is not good practice
s: Applying a fixed emission factor directly to cement production is not good practice because it ignores clinker imports and exports.

loc.section: TIER 1 METHOD: ESTIMATING CLINKER PRODUCTION THROUGH USE OF CEMENT PRODUCTION DATA

n: Double counting rule for soda ash use
s: Soda ash used in glass production is reported under glass production, not under other uses of soda ash.

n: Energy and IPPU boundary for calcination emissions
s: IPPU covers only calcination emissions, while fuel combustion emissions, including from waste fuels, belong to the Energy Sector.

n: Fraction calcination default for glass carbonates
s: If the calcination fraction for a particulate carbonate is unknown, it may be assumed to be 1.00.

n: Full documentation of lime Tier 3 underlying information
s: Tier 3 must document all underlying information; reporting only final emissions is not good practice.

n: Glass cullet ratio ranges and mid-point use
s: Cullet ratios vary within and across countries; mid-point values of provided ranges should be used unless another value is known to be more representative.

n: Glass reporting of mineral wool emissions
s: Rock wool emissions are reported under IPCC Subcategory 2A5, slag-related emissions go to the metallurgical category, and slag re-melting for mineral wool need not be reported.
Glass production data reported in units other than mass, such as bottles or square metres, should be converted to tonnes.

n: Hydrated lime correction data availability rule
s: Hydrated lime correction is good practice under Tier 2 and, where data exist, Tier 1; with no Tier 1 data, hydrated lime production is assumed zero.

loc.section: CORRECTION FOR THE PROPORTION OF HYDRATED LIME

s: Emissions from imported clinker are excluded from national estimates, while emissions from exported clinker are included in the producing country.

loc.section: TIER 1 METHOD: ESTIMATING CLINKER PRODUCTION THROUGH USE OF CEMENT PRODUCTION DATA

n: Lime and glass reporting of separate emissions and reductions
s: When reporting CO2 recovery under Category 2H, emissions and emission reductions must be reported separately, not only net lime emissions.

n: Lime and glass time series consistency
s: The same method should be used for every year of the lime time series; missing historical years may be estimated by interpolation, trend extrapolation, or holding the current proportion constant.

n: Lime emission factor uncertainty for hydraulic lime
s: Emission factor uncertainty is 15 percent for hydraulic lime and 2 percent for other lime types.

n: Lime production completeness and double counting
s: All lime production, marketed or non-marketed, should be reported, and compilers must avoid double counting with carbonate consumption and hydrated lime.
Where uncertainty values are given as ranges, the mid-range should be used unless country-specific or plant-specific circumstances suggest another value.
Activity data should include both marketed and non-marketed lime; no default value is provided for non-marketed lime quantities.

n: Other process uses of carbonates method selection rule
s: The Tier 3 method for other process uses of carbonates should only be applied at the plant level, and Tier 1 or 2 may be combined with Tier 3 across sub-categories.
Recarbonation may be calculated and reported only where proven and validated methods are used.

n: Reporting documentation requirement for carbonate process emissions
s: The inventory should include method summaries and source data references so that emission estimates are transparent and reproducible, and Tier 1/2 breakdown defaults must be documented.

n: Reporting location rule for other process uses of carbonates
s: Emissions from carbonate consumption should be reported in the source category where the carbonate is consumed and CO2 emitted.

n: Reporting of marketed and non-marketed lime under subcategory 2A2
s: All lime production, marketed or non-marketed, should be reported under IPCC Subcategory 2A2 Lime Production.

n: Reporting rule for emissions from other process uses of carbonates
s: Emissions from other process uses of carbonates should be reported in the source category where the carbonates are consumed.
Soda ash is treated as sodium carbonate, so Tier 1 uses the sodium carbonate emission factor instead of the 85/15 limestone-dolomite fraction.

For sugar refining, emissions from lime production at sugar mills are reported under 2A2 Lime Production, other emissions under 2A4 Other Process Uses of Carbonates, and removals under 2H2 Food and Beverages Industry.
Absent disaggregated data, Tier 1 assumes 85 percent high-calcium lime and 15 percent dolomitic lime, with zero hydraulic lime unless other information is available.

n: Tier 1 lime method has no LKD correction
s: The Tier 1 lime method does not correct for LKD.

n: Tier 3 activity data scope: kiln carbonate inputs only
s: Activity data for Tier 3 include only carbonates fed into the kiln; carbonates added in the finish mill are excluded because they are not calcined.

n: Tier 3 uncertainty of raw material weighing
s: Uncertainty of weighing or proportioning raw materials under Tier 3 is about 1-3 percent, and glass Tier 1 and 2 activity data are roughly ±5 percent.

n: Time series consistency for carbonate reporting
s: Time series consistency requires using the same data sources for all years, with interpolation or surrogate methods where data are missing for some years.
The LKD correction factor for vertical shaft kilns is judged negligible and need not be estimated.

n: Abatement factor use with default emission factors
s: Default emission factors already include abatement effects where relevant, and inventory compilers should verify abatement is installed and operated throughout the year.
The acetonitrile and hydrogen cyanide secondary product factors apply only to acrylonitrile production from propylene feedstock.

n: Activity data basis for nitric acid N2O estimates
s: Nitric acid activity data should be expressed as 100 percent HNO3.

n: Activity data precision and default uncertainty
s: Plant-level production data are typically accurate to ±2 percent, and a default activity data uncertainty of ±2 percent may be used when no other value is available.

n: Activity data uncertainty default for TiO2 production
s: Where uncertainty values are unavailable, a default activity data uncertainty of ±5 percent may be used.
Emissions from the CaO step are reported as lime production, and only the CaO-petroleum coke reaction and acetylene welding use are reported as calcium carbide emissions.

n: Ammonia CO2 generation rate sanity check
s: CO2 generation rate from natural gas-based ammonia should not be below 1.14 tonnes CO2 per tonne ammonia.

n: Applicability of EDC/VCM default CH4 factor
s: The Table 3.19 default CH4 factor is not applicable to stand-alone EDC production plants.

n: Applicability of Tier 2 and Tier 3 HFC-23 methods
s: Tier 2 and Tier 3 HFC-23 methods are suitable only for plant-level calculations, and Tier 1 or 2 may fill plants without Tier 3 data.

n: Averaging rule for carbon and fluorine balance emission factors
s: The emission factor used in Equation 3.31 should normally be the average of the carbon and fluorine balance based factors unless overriding documented considerations apply.
Biogenic methanol included in national statistics can overestimate fossil methanol CO2 unless production activity data are adjusted.
Plant-level (bottom-up) estimates should be compared with national production-based (top-down) estimates and unexplained discrepancies investigated.

loc.section: Comparison of emissions estimates using different approaches

n: Capacity utilisation factor for nitric acid Tier 1 fallback
s: When national production data are unavailable, national capacity is multiplied by an 80 percent ±10 percent utilisation factor.

n: Caprolactam activity data production capacity fallback
s: Tier 1 activity data may be national production capacity multiplied by a capacity utilisation factor of 80 percent ± 20 percent when national production is unavailable.
Default factors should be used only where plant-specific measurements are not available, and the default is considered uncertain for caprolactam.

n: Carbon black biogenic and refinery production boundary
s: Biogenic carbon black may inflate fossil carbon black statistics, and carbon black made inside refineries should be reported as chemical industry process emissions.
The default assumption is no CO2 capture and storage; where capture is used, good practice is to deduct captured CO2 in a higher tier calculation.

n: CO2 recovered for urea production deduction rule
s: CO2 recovered for urea production is estimated as urea production times 44/60, and emissions from urea use must be accounted for elsewhere when deducted.

n: Completeness check via national mass balance
s: Initial national mass-balance estimates should identify whether smaller producers and recycling firms make a sizeable contribution to emissions.

n: Consistent time series method for production emissions
s: By-product and fugitive emissions should use the same method and appropriate factors across the entire time series.

n: Default activity data uncertainty for soda ash
s: When no uncertainty values are available from other sources, a default activity data uncertainty of ±5 percent can be used.

n: Default assumption of no CO2 capture and storage in ammonia production
s: The default assumption is that no CO2 capture and storage takes place, and captured CO2 should be deducted in higher tier calculations.

n: Default emission factors for TiO2 production (Table 3.9)
s: Default CO2 factors for synthetic rutile and chloride-route rutile TiO2 are given with uncertainties; titanium slag has no default.

n: Default factors use condition for adipic acid abatement
s: Default factors should be used only where plant-specific measurements are unavailable, and only after verifying abatement technology is installed and operated throughout the year.

n: Default uncertainty values for Tier 1 production emissions
s: Default activity data uncertainty is about 1 percent for well-operated facilities, and default emission factor uncertainty is 100 percent.

n: Documentation and archiving requirements for caprolactam N2O
s: Method description, plant counts, factors, production data, capacity, abatement details and assumptions should be documented and archived, with plant-level records kept confidential where needed.

n: Double counting adjustment for TiO2 reductant and carbothermal inputs
s: Electrode carbon, reductant coal and chloride-route petroleum coke must be subtracted from energy and non-energy use reported in the Energy Sector to avoid double counting.

n: Double counting avoidance between IPPU and Energy Sector for ammonia feedstock

s: Table 5.5 gives default land-use, tillage (management) and carbon input factors, relative to nominal reference conditions, by climate and moisture regime.

n: Table 5.6 annual emission factors for cultivated organic soils
s: Table 5.6 gives default annual emission factors for cultivated organic soils by temperature regime, with a nominal error of plus or minus 90 percent.

n: Tier 1 below-ground biomass default for perennial trees in agricultural systems
s: At Tier 1 below-ground biomass change of perennial trees in agricultural systems is assumed zero and no default below-ground values are provided.

n: Tier 1 default above-ground woody biomass coefficients by climate region
s: Table 5.1 gives default above-ground biomass stock at harvest, harvest cycle, accumulation rate G and loss L by climate region for perennial cropping systems.

n: Tier 1 default assumption for dead organic matter after conversion to Cropland
s: Under Tier 1, dead wood and litter stocks are assumed fully lost on conversion and not replenished on cropland.

n: Tier 1 DOM pool stability assumption for cropland
s: The source states that Tier 1 assumes dead wood and litter stocks are absent or at equilibrium in cropland, so no DOM change estimate is needed.

n: Tier 3 validation requirement for rice CH4 models
s: Tier 3 models must be validated with independent observations from country or region-specific studies covering the range of rice cultivation characteristics.

n: Time dependence of Land Converted to Cropland
s: Land remains classified as Land Converted to Cropland for 20 years, which affects how inventory periods shorter than 20 years are assigned.

n: Total land area consistency across land-use sectors
s: The total land area across all land-use sectors must remain equal over the inventory period when land is converted.

n: Aggregate activity data (Approach 1) limitation for cropland-to-grassland soil C
s: With Approach 1 aggregate data, previous land use before conversion is unknown and cultivated annual cropland converted to grassland cannot be determined, which may overestimate C gain over 20 years especially with Tier 1; this caveat should be documented.

n: Annual data for non-CO2 biomass burning emissions
s: The source requires countries to report non-CO2 biomass burning emissions in grassland using annual data rather than period averages.

loc.section: 6.2.4 Non-CO_2 greenhouse gas emissions from biomass burning

n: Area averaging rule for multi-year conversion periods
s: Conversion areas assessed over multi-year periods must be converted to average annual areas to match annual carbon stock values.

n: Area-based conversion data requirements for grassland conversion
s: Area estimates of conversions to grassland must be consistent across pools and disaggregated, with forest conversions identified separately as a minimum requirement.

n: Area burnt estimation must be validated
s: Estimation of area burnt is critical for non-CO2 emissions; remote-sensed estimates must be tested against ground data and regional average statistics are likely unreliable for a specific country.

n: Carbon content of dry biomass (Tier 2 default)
s: The Tier 2 default carbon content is 0.50 t C per t dry woody biomass and 0.47 t C per t dry herbaceous biomass.

n: Carry-over of stocks between reporting periods
s: Starting C stocks in a reporting period for lands converted to grassland must equal the stock state reported previously, e.g. transferred biomass carried to the dead organic matter pool.

n: Consistent time series of classifications and factors
s: Compilers should apply the same classifications and factors over the entire inventory period, and the land base should remain consistent except for conversions.

n: Dead organic matter carbon fraction defaults
s: Default carbon fractions for dead wood and litter in grassland DOM are 0.50 and 0.40 t C per t d.m., with litter ranging 0.05–0.50 in the literature.

n: Default biomass immediately after conversion for Tier 1
s: For Tier 1 the default biomass immediately after conversion is 0 tonne per hectare because all biomass is assumed cleared.

n: Default biomass of cropland with annual crops before conversion
s: For Tier 1, cropland with annual crops is given a default biomass of 4.7 tonnes of carbon per hectare or 10 tonnes dry matter per hectare with error of plus 75 percent.

n: Default carbon content of woody and herbaceous biomass
s: The source gives default carbon content of 0.50 t C per t dry biomass for woody biomass and 0.47 for herbaceous biomass in the Tier 2 biomass method.

n: Default carbon fractions for biomass and dead organic matter in land converted to grassland
s: IPCC default carbon fractions for woody and herbaceous biomass, dead wood and litter used in the conversion-to-grassland methods.

n: Default root-to-shoot expansion factors R for grassland (Table 6.1)
s: Table 6.1 gives default below-ground to above-ground biomass ratios R by grassland vegetation type and approximate IPCC climate zone, used when country-specific values are unavailable.

n: Documentation and archiving requirements for grassland inventories
s: Good practice is to document and archive all information needed to produce inventory estimates, including activity data, processing procedures, definitions and expert knowledge use.

n: Internal and external QA/QC for grassland inventories
s: Good practice requires internal review of the implementation process and external review by independent parties, including checks that total land areas stay constant across the time series.

n: Land base area balance for Land Converted to Grassland
s: The total land area accounted across all land-use sectors must remain equal over the inventory period, so conversions add area to one sector and remove it from others.

n: Mineral soil organic carbon Tier 1 approach
s: Tier 1 mineral soil SOC change is estimated from SOC at the start and end of the inventory period divided by the time dependence D of stock change factors, with exposed bedrock assigned a stock of zero.

n: Minimum activity data for soil C in Land Converted to Grassland
s: Countries need at minimum estimates of areas of Land Converted to Grassland during the inventory period, stratified by climate region and soil type.

n: Non-CO2 reporting for biomass burning on managed grassland
s: Non-CO2 greenhouse gases should be reported for all controlled burns and wildfires on managed grasslands, including forest-to-grassland conversion.

n: Omission of management practices must be documented
s: When management practice effects cannot be estimated, countries may inventory land use alone but must clearly identify the omission in reporting documentation.
Tier 1 estimates grassland organic soil C change by stratifying managed organic soils by climate region, applying climate-specific annual emission rates, and excluding undrained natural grasslands.

n: Recalculation when country-specific factors are introduced
s: New country-specific factors should be applied across the entire inventory and the time series recalculated; if full data are unavailable, the effect of activity changes versus data or method changes should be demonstrated.

n: Reporting of biomass burning emissions for cropland-to-grassland conversion
s: Cropland conversion to grassland does not normally involve biomass burning, but any such emissions should be reported annually when practiced.

loc.section: 6.3.4 Non-CO_2 greenhouse gas emissions from biomass burning

n: Reporting of CO2 net release from fire-driven woody change
s: Where fire management changes the grass–woody balance, net CO2 release caused by burning should also be reported because re-fixation may not offset emissions in the short term.

n: Stratification of activity data for biomass burning in Land Converted to Grassland
s: Area converted to Grassland must be stratified by Forest Land-converted and Cropland-converted, since fuel availability varies by prior land use.

n: Table 6.2 relative stock change factors for grassland management
s: Table 6.2 gives default land-use, management and input factors (with error ranges) used to scale reference soil C stocks in Tier 1 grassland stock change estimates.

n: Table 6.3 annual emission factors for drained grassland organic soils
s: Table 6.3 gives default annual C loss emission factors for drained grassland on organic soils by climate regime, with error of plus or minus 90 percent.

n: Tier 1 biomass loss assumption for biomass burning in Land Converted to Grassland
s: Under Tier 1, all above-ground biomass and DOM in the previous land use is assumed lost immediately after conversion.

n: Tier 1 combustion and emission factors for biomass burning
s: Tier 1 uses default combustion factors from Table 2.6 and default emission factors from Table 2.5 in Chapter 2 for each non-CO2 gas.
Tier 1 assumes no change in biomass in Grassland Remaining Grassland, so no biomass worksheet is needed.

n: Tier 1 steady-state assumption for dead organic matter
s: Tier 1 assumes dead wood and litter stocks are at equilibrium, so no DOM stock change is estimated and no worksheet is provided.
For Tier 3 model-based approaches, good practice is to document model versions and descriptions and archive model inputs, source code and executables.

n: Tier requirement for biomass burning emissions as key category
s: Countries should use Tier 2 or Tier 3 for biomass burning emissions in Land Converted to Grassland whenever this is a key category.

n: Tier selection for biomass burning non-CO2 emissions
s: If biomass burning in Grassland Remaining Grassland is not a key category, Tier 1 may be used; if it is a key category, the highest feasible Tier should be applied.

n: Transition period for Land Converted to Grassland
s: A 20-year transition period following conversion is the default period before converted land is moved into Grassland Remaining Grassland, and countries may choose another period.

n: Transition period for land converted to grassland
s: Land converted to grassland is tracked in annual cohorts for a default 20-year transition period before moving to Grassland Remaining Grassland.

n: Uncertainty sources for land converted to grassland
s: Uncertainty analysis for Land Converted to Grassland follows the same approach as Grassland Remaining Grassland and has two sources.

n: Activity data for land converted to peat extraction (Tier 2 and Tier 3)
s: Tier 2 requires area of organic soils converted for peat extraction disaggregated by nutrient status; Tier 3 requires detailed original land use, peat type and fertility.

n: Activity data requirements for peatland CO2 and N2O estimation
s: All tiers require areas of peatlands managed for peat extraction and air-dry peat production data by weight or volume, and the same activity data should be used for CO2 and N2O.

n: Boundary between Peatlands Remaining Peatlands and Land Being Converted for Peat Extraction
s: Emissions from peatlands undergoing extraction differ from land-conversion emissions, so countries with active peat industries should separate managed peatlands accordingly.

n: Default-factor choice by peatland fertility and climate
s: Where fertility split is unknown, boreal countries use the nutrient-poor factor and temperate countries use the nutrient-rich factor under Tier 1.

n: Default transition period for Land Being Converted for Peat Extraction
s: The recommended default transition period for land being converted for peat extraction is five years, unlike other land-use conversions in the Guidelines.

loc.section: 7.2.2 Land Being Converted for Peat Extraction

n: Double-counting avoidance for biomass clearing and horticultural peat N2O
s: Tier 2 methods must avoid double-counting CO2 from biomass clearing, and the default N2O approach excludes decay of organic nitrogen in horticultural peat.

n: Flooded Land Remaining Flooded Land methodology
s: No methodologies are provided for Flooded Land Remaining Flooded Land; only CO2 from conversion to flooded land is covered.

n: Off-site energy use of peat is excluded from Chapter 7
s: Off-site emissions from peat used for energy are reported in the Energy Sector and are not included in the wetlands chapter estimates.

n: Peatlands remain managed after peat extraction ceases
s: Peatlands under peat extraction remain managed peatlands after extraction stops until converted to another use; rewetting does not change this status.

n: Scope of N2O emissions from Flooded Lands
s: N2O emissions from Flooded Lands are not considered in this section to avoid double-counting with anthropogenic sources.

n: Scope of wetland N2O default methodology
s: A default N2O methodology is provided only for peatlands managed for peat extraction.

n: Tier 1 default carbon fractions of air-dry peat (Table 7.5)
s: Table 7.5 gives default carbon fractions by weight and by volume for converting peat production data to carbon by climate zone.

n: Tier 1 default CO2 emission factors for managed peatlands by fertility
s: Table 7.4 gives default CO2-C emission factors for peat extraction lands in boreal/temperate (nutrient-poor and nutrient-rich) and tropical zones, with uncertainty ranges.

n: Tier 1 default N2O emission factors for managed peatlands (Table 7.6)
s: Table 7.6 gives default N2O emission factors for managed peatlands by climate zone and fertility.
Default uncertainty for peatland CO2 emissions is the 95% interval of a log-normal distribution rather than a symmetric standard deviation.
Some wetland uses such as manure ponds, industrial effluent ponds, aquaculture ponds, and rewetting or restoration are not covered due to lack of methodologies.

n: Active growing period zero-increment assumption for urban trees
s: For Tiers 2a and 2b, ΔC_L is assumed zero where average tree age is 20 years or less, and older trees have increment offset by loss.

n: Carbon fraction default for dry matter conversion in Tier 3
s: When biomass is measured on a dry matter basis, a default carbon fraction of 0.5 tonne C per tonne dry matter applies unless a more appropriate value is used.

n: Carbon fraction for dead wood and litter in Settlements
s: The Guidelines give carbon fraction values of 0.50 for dead wood and 0.40 for litter when country-specific data are unavailable.

n: Carbon fraction of dead wood and litter default
s: A default carbon fraction of 0.50 tonne C per tonne dry matter is given for dead wood and litter.

n: Consistent land base and time series
s: Countries must apply the same inventory methods across the full reporting period and keep total land area consistent across years, re-calculating the series when methods change.

n: Dead organic matter assumption at Tier 1
s: Tier 1 assumes dead wood and litter stocks are at equilibrium, so no carbon stock change is estimated for these pools.

n: Expansion factor requirement for Stock-Difference Method
s: Tier 3 requires country- or region-specific expansion factors, while Tier 2 has no default expansion factors and requires best available local data documented.
The conservative approach sets the litter component of DOM accumulation rate to zero.

n: Minimum forest conversion disaggregation requirement for Settlements
s: For consistency with the IPCC Guidelines, areas of Forest Land converted to Settlements must be identified separately.

n: Organic soil drainage in settlements Tier 1
s: If settlement soils are drained and peat not removed, emissions use cultivated organic soil emission factors; if peat removed, carbon is released in year of removal.

n: Organic soil treatment for conversions to Settlements
s: Land converted to Settlements on organic soils is treated the same as Settlements Remaining Settlements for Tiers 1 and 2, with carbon losses from Equation 2.26.
Settlements emissions map to specified IPCC reporting categories (5A, 5B, 5D, 5E, 4D, 4E, 4F) depending on remaining or converted land and pool.

n: Root-to-shoot ratio default for urban tree below-ground biomass
s: Below-ground tree biomass may be estimated separately using a root:shoot ratio of 0.26 when required.

n: Settlement area stratification for Tier 1 soil carbon
s: Converted area must be stratified by climate region and soil type for Tier 1, and absent specific information, paved area is estimated from non-greenspace proportion using Table 8.3.

n: Table 8.4 default biomass carbon stocks removed due to land conversion to Settlements
s: Table 8.4 gives default pre-conversion biomass carbon stocks per land-use category, with forest and grassland values deferred to other chapters and cropland given as a single default with error range.

n: Tier 1 biomass assumption for settlements remaining settlements
s: Tier 1 assumes no change in biomass carbon stocks in Settlements Remaining Settlements, and uncertainty assessment is not required for living biomass at Tier 1.
Tiers 2a and 2b assume no change in herbaceous biomass, so herbaceous growth is taken as equal to loss.

n: Tier 2a default CRW for urban tree crown cover by region
s: Default crown cover area-based growth rates for urban trees are 2.9 for the United States (global default) and 3.6 for Australia, in tonnes C per ha crown cover per year.
Area estimates of land converted to Other Land must cover a time period consistent with land-use surveys and the land-use change matrix, and the same aggregate areas are used for biomass and soil.

n: Consistent time series for Other Land
s: Countries should apply the same inventory methods, definitions and climate/soil types over the entire reporting period, recalculating when methods change.

n: Dead organic matter for Tiers 1 and 2 on conversion to Other Land
s: For Tiers 1 and 2, all biomass and dead organic matter carbon is assumed emitted in the year of conversion, with no DOM accumulation.

n: Reporting category for soil CO2 from Land Converted to Other Land
s: CO2 emissions and removals from soils resulting from Land Converted to Other Land are reported in IPCC Reporting Category 5D, changes in soil carbon.

n: Soil carbon Tier 1 decline to zero after conversion
s: At Tier 1 soil carbon is assumed to decline to zero after conversion; if not the case, the land should probably be classified under another Other Land use.

n: Tier 1 biomass default: all biomass carbon released in first year
s: The Tier 1 biomass calculation sets B_AFTER to zero and assumes all biomass carbon (less harvested wood products) is released in the first year after conversion.

n: Tier 2 biomass: country-specific B_BEFORE, B_AFTER zero
s: Tier 2 biomass estimation requires country-specific pre-conversion carbon stocks, keeps B_AFTER at zero, and can apportion losses to burning or harvesting.

n: Activity data and documentation requirements for manure N2O inventories
s: Good practice requires documenting activity data, manure management system data, emission factors and, for Tier 2, VS/Bo and MCF or N-related components used.

n: Activity data characterisation level by method
s: Tier 1 default factors need only a basic livestock population characterisation, whereas gross-energy-intake based estimation needs a Tier 2 characterisation.
Inventory compilers should use official national statistics or industry population data, with FAO data as fallback, and must document population estimation adjustments.

loc.section: TIER 1: B ASIC CHARACTERISATION FOR LIVESTOCK POPULATIONS

n: Burned dung N split and reporting category
s: For manure burned for fuel, about half of excreted N is assumed in dung and half in urine, and emissions are reported under Energy or Waste categories depending on energy recovery.
Default pregnancy coefficients are 0.10 for cattle and buffalo and 0.077, 0.126 and 0.150 for sheep with single, double and triple or more births.

n: CO2 emissions from livestock not estimated
s: CO2 emissions from livestock are not estimated in this chapter because annual net CO2 emissions are assumed to be zero.

n: Consistent methane conversion factors over time
s: Methane conversion factors used over a time series must be consistent and must reflect changes in farm practice or mitigation measures, with the changes explained in the inventory text.

loc.section: 10.3.5 Completeness, Time series, Quality Assurance/Quality Control and Reporting

n: Coordinated livestock characterisation across source categories
s: A coordinated livestock characterisation must be used across enteric fermentation, manure CH4, manure N2O and managed soil N2O categories to ensure consistency.

n: Coordination of manure N with managed soils reporting
s: Manure N applied after storage or treatment must be reported under N2O from managed soils, with the same N excretion rates used for manure management.

loc.section: 10.5.4 Coordination with reporting for N_2 O emissions from managed soils

s: The source gives default uncertainty ranges for dairy cow mass, Bo and VS production used in the MCF/EF derivation.

loc.section: Annex 10A.2 Data underlying methane default emission factors for Manure Management

n: Dairy cow manure system MCF for lagoon and liquid/slurry
s: The source states that lagoon and liquid/slurry MCFs follow the van't Hoff-Arrhenius relation to temperature and that lagoon MCFs also depend on retention time up to a year.

loc.section: Annex 10A.2 Data underlying methane default emission factors for Manure Management

n: Double counting and reporting boundary for manure N2O
s: Manure N2O from pasture, range and paddock is reported under managed soils, and manure N losses must be excluded from manure N available for soil application to avoid double counting.

loc.section: 10.5 N_2 O EMISSIONS FROM MANURE MANAGEMENT

s: Natural wild ruminants are excluded from a country's emission estimate, and only domestically managed animals are considered.

n: Full-year vs shorter-period emission factor period
s: The Equation 10.21 emission factor assumes 365 days, and is replaced by the number of days in a shorter defined period such as a wet season or 150-day feedlot period.

n: Key species significance rule of thumb
s: As a rule of thumb, a livestock species is significant if it accounts for 25-30% or more of emissions from the source category.

n: Manure management method choice (Tier 1 versus Tier 2 and Tier 3)
s: The method depends on data availability; Tier 2 is good practice and Tier 1 should be used only after Tier 2 avenues are exhausted or the source is not key.

n: Manure management system usage uncertainty and derivation rule
s: Uncertainty of MMS usage data ranges from 10% or less for single-system countries to 25–50% where many systems are used.

loc.section: ACTIVITY DATA – MANURE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM USAGE

n: Manure N loss rates apply only to typical housing and storage without controls
s: Default total N loss values represent average typical components without significant N control measures, so alternative rates are needed where controls exist.

loc.section: EMISSION FACTORS – DIRECT N_2 O EMISSIONS

n: Market swine and breeding swine default uncertainty ranges
s: The source gives default uncertainty ranges for market swine and breeding swine mass, Bo and VS production.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories 10.78

n: Mitigation technology inclusion in Tier 2/3 inventories
s: Mitigation technologies should be reflected only if they meet QA/QC, have international acceptance, show take-up evidence, and are supported by peer-reviewed publications.

loc.section: Potential for refinement of Tier 2 or development of a Tier 3 method to e nteric methane emission inventories

s: The source gives default uncertainty ranges for other cattle mass, Bo and VS production.

loc.section: Annex 10A.2 Data underlying methane default emission factors for Manure Management

n: Reporting category allocation for manure management N2O
s: N2O from manure management is reported under Manure Management except pasture/range/paddock manure (managed soils) and manure burned for fuel or incineration.

n: Significance threshold for a livestock species
s: As a rule of thumb, a livestock species is significant if it accounts for 25-30% or more of emissions from the source category.
Table 10.2 gives guideline digestibility ranges (DE%) for swine, cattle and other ruminants, and poultry by class; local measured data are preferred.
Table 10.4 gives the Cf_i values in MJ d-1 kg-1 by animal category used in the NE_m equation.
Table 10.5 gives feeding-situation activity coefficients C_a for cattle, buffalo and sheep.
Table 10.6 gives constants a and b for sheep net energy for growth by category, sourced from AFRC (1993).

n: Temperature range rule for liquid-based MCF values
s: Areas with annual average temperatures outside 10–28 °C must use the end-of-range MCF values or develop country-specific values.
Using the same Tier 1 emission factors across successive years ignores changing livestock productivity, which may require a Tier 2 calculation if the trend matters.

n: Tier 1 livestock method selection and sheep Ym by age
s: Suggested enteric fermentation inventory method per livestock type, and Ym for sheep by age.
When Tier 2 is used, the inventory must report values of Y_m, DE values and full documentation of data and references.

n: Tier 2 uncertainty and dry/liquid classification rule
s: Solid versus liquid/slurry classification uses quantitative data with a 20% dry matter borderline.

n: Tier classification for manure N2O methods
s: Tier 1 uses IPCC default factors, excretion and system data; Tier 2 uses the same equations with some or all country-specific variables; Tier 3 uses alternative country-specific procedures such as mass balance.

n: Time series consistency for manure N and emission parameters
s: Parameters and emission factors must reflect changes in practice, and the inventory must explain how changes affected the time series.

loc.section: 10.5.6 Completeness, Time series, Quality assurance/Quality control and Reporting

s: For open-lot fed cattle in colder climates, Cf_i is adjusted upward by 0.0048 per degree C below 20 C.

n: Zero methane conversion factor for milk-only juveniles
s: A CH4 conversion factor of zero is assumed for juveniles consuming only milk.

n: Averaging lime activity data over three years
s: If emissions are not computed annually for reporting, good practice is to average lime data over the current year and two most recent years.

n: Consistency of urea application data between CO2 and N2O
s: Annual urea application estimates used for CO2 from urea should be consistent with those used for N2O emissions from soils.

n: Default emission factor for urea CO2 (Tier 1)
s: The Tier 1 default emission factor for carbon emissions from urea applications is 0.20 tonne C per tonne urea.

n: Default emission factors for liming CO2 (Tier 1)
s: Tier 1 default emission factors for carbonate lime are 0.12 for limestone and 0.13 for dolomite, expressed as tonne C per tonne of material.

n: EF2 and EF3PRP default values by climate and animal type
s: Text gives EF2 defaults for temperate and tropical climates and EF3PRP defaults by animal type.
Frac_LEACH-(H) defaults to 0.30 in humid regions or dryland regions with non-drip irrigation, and is zero for other regions where leaching is unlikely.
Reported N2O mass is obtained from N2O-N by multiplying by 44/28.

n: Oxide and hydroxide lime excluded from liming CO2 calculation
s: Oxides and hydroxides of lime contain no inorganic carbon and are excluded from the soil liming CO2 calculation.
A sub-source category is treated as significant if it accounts for 25-30% of emissions from its source category, as a rule of thumb.

n: Sources of N for indirect N2O emissions from agricultural inputs
s: The methodology covers five agricultural N sources for indirect N2O: synthetic fertiliser, organic fertiliser, grazing urine and dung, crop residues, and SOM mineralisation.

n: Stability of N2O factors across time series
s: Frac_GASF, Frac_GASM, Frac_LEACH, EF_4 and EF_5 should not change interannually unless mitigation is undertaken, and changes require justification.

n: Table 11.1 default emission factors for direct N2O from managed soils
s: Table 11.1 gives default EF values and uncertainty ranges for direct N2O emissions from managed soils.

n: Tier 1 applicability and tier selection for direct N2O
s: Tier 1 uses default factors without land cover, soil, climate or management differentiation, and countries with data showing defaults are inappropriate should use Tier 2 or Tier 3 with full explanation.

loc.section: 11.2 N_2 O EMISSIONS FROM MANAGED SOILS

n: Urea CO2 emission factor upper bound on uncertainty
s: The uncertainty applied to the urea emission factor cannot exceed the default factor because it is the absolute maximum emission.
Tier 1 inventories are complete only if emissions are based on full accounting of all urea applied to soils.

n: Volatilisation adjustment rule for Tier 1 N inputs
s: For Tier 1, applied mineral and organic N are not adjusted for NH3 and NOx volatilisation, while Tier 2 and 3 may require such correction.

n: Waste N input under F_ON in Equation 11.1
s: Waste N added as a sub-term under F_ON is measured in N units and multiplied by EF_1, and sewage sludge requires a cross-check with the Waste Sector to avoid double counting.

n: AFA system boundary for AFOLU CO2 emissions
s: Under the Atmospheric Flow Approach, the AFOLU CO2 emissions in the national boundary are defined by Equation 12A.3 with the stated carbon flow terms.

loc.section: Figure 12.A.2 System boundary of the Atmospheric Flow Approach.

n: Bark expansion factor for HWP harvest
s: The source states a default bark expansion factor of 1.13 to convert FAO harvest values to total harvest including bark.

n: Double-counting boundary between AFOLU, Energy, and Waste sectors for HWP
s: HWP CO2 release is included in AFOLU, wood burned for energy is excluded from Energy totals, and CO2 from SWDS is excluded from Waste totals while CH4 is included.

loc.section: 1 All CO_2 released from HWP is included in the AFOLU Sector;

n: Exclusion of wood-based final products from Tier 1 and Tier 2 trade data
s: Trade in final wood-based products such as prefabricated houses, furniture and books is not in FAO statistics and is excluded from Tier 1 and 2 methods to avoid double-counting.

loc.section: 2 The estimation method is a simplification of real world processes.

s: The guidance assumes amount of woody material in use declines by first-order decay; other decay profiles such as linear decay are possible alternatives.
A negative HWP Contribution decreases AFOLU emissions and a positive value increases them.

loc.section: 5 Annual harvest for wood products in the reporting country 5 (Gg of carbon per year).

n: HWP reporting in AFOLU background Table 3.10 (Table 12.7)
s: Good practice is to report HWP contribution, approach, harvested/imported/exported amounts and CO2 release in Table 12.7 even when HWP contribution is zero.

n: HWP reporting-year coverage for annual estimates
s: Tiered methods provide annual estimates for any year from 1990 to the current year.

loc.section: 5 Annual harvest for wood products in the reporting country 5 (Gg of carbon per year).

n: Mutual exclusivity of HWP accounting approaches
s: Alternative HWP contribution approaches are mutually exclusive, so a global or regional estimate is correct only if all countries use the same approach.

n: Pre-1961 backward extrapolation of HWP data
s: The source states that consumption and related variables before 1961 are estimated by backward extrapolation using regional rates of change, with FAO data from 1961 onward.

n: Production Approach system boundary note on exports
s: Under the Production Approach only HWP exports made from domestic roundwood are within the system boundary, not those processed domestically from imported roundwood.

loc.section: Figure 12.A.3 System boundary of the Production Approach.

n: Products in use and SWDS reporting boundary for Stock-Change approach
s: Stock-change changes are reported by the producing country for forest pools and by the consuming country for product pools, so the report must indicate when and where stock changes occur.

loc.section: Figure 12.A.1 System boundary of the Stock-Change approach.

n: Starting year 1900 for HWP stock history
s: Inputs and outputs since 1900 are recommended for estimating existing HWP stock, with pre-1900 contributions judged insignificant.
Tier choice depends on availability of country-specific data and methods, not on whether HWP is a key category.
The HWP Contribution may be reported as zero when the annual change in HWP carbon stocks is judged insignificant, replacing the 1996 IPCC guidance.

n: Default inventory time period for stock change factors
s: The default time dependence for stock change factors is 20 years, and T is used instead when T exceeds D.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.25

n: Initial land use fallback rule in IPCC worksheets
s: When data by initial land use are unavailable, the worksheet column must be filled using only the non-wetland, non-settlement, or non-other-land category as specified in each worksheet.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.37

s: The liming worksheet gives default carbon emission factors of 0.12 tonnes C per tonne limestone and 0.13 tonnes C per tonne dolomite.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.54

s: Manure N calculations must be done per manure management system, with the relevant livestock categories selected for each system.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.61

s: Each subcategory must be reported on a separate line for each non-CO2 greenhouse gas.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.49

s: Rice harvested area must be disaggregated at least into irrigated, rainfed and upland baseline water regimes, with sub-strata for each organic amendment type.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.63

n: Sheet unit and disaggregation rules for direct N2O worksheet
s: Organic soil areas must be disaggregated by cropland/grassland, forest, temperate, tropical, nutrient rich and nutrient poor categories, and animal N inputs by CPP and SO.

loc.section: 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories A1.57

n: Tier 1 worksheet availability for land-use based C stock changes

s: Wastewater is excluded from fossil liquid waste unless incinerated, and biogenic liquid waste need not be accounted for unless mixed with fossil oil carrying a significant fossil carbon portion.

s: Emissions from waste incineration without energy recovery are reported in the Waste Sector and those with energy recovery in the Energy Sector, and the chapter's methodology applies to both.

n: CH4 recovery inclusion rule for industrial wastewater

n: Time series consistency for wastewater CH4 estimates

n: Units consistency between TOW and B_o
s: TOW and B_o must be based on the same units (either BOD or COD) to calculate emissions.

n: Double-counting avoidance for transferred IPPU fuels
s: When IPPU-derived fuels are transferred to the energy sector, the transferred quantity is noted as an information item under the IPPU category and reported in the relevant energy category to avoid double counting.

n: IPPU–Energy demarcation of fuel combustion emissions
s: Combustion emissions from fuels derived from an IPPU feedstock are normally allocated to the IPPU process source category, unless the derived fuels are transferred for combustion elsewhere, in which case they are reported in the energy sector.

n: Mobile combustion for energy carrier transport
s: Combustion emissions from transporting energy carriers by ship, rail and road are included in mobile combustion processes rather than fugitive emissions.

n: Territorial allocation of oil and gas production emissions
s: Combustion and fugitive emissions from production, processing and handling of oil and gas should be allocated according to the national territory of the facilities, including offshore areas, which may be an agreed economic zone.

n: Biomass CO2 information item in Energy sector
s: CO2 from combustion of biomass for energy is estimated in the Energy sector but recorded as an information item excluded from the sectoral total.
Only the part of biomass combusted for energy purposes is estimated for the Energy sector information item.

n: CH4 and N2O from biomass combustion in Energy totals
s: CH4 and N2O from combustion of biomass for energy are included in the Energy sector totals.

n: Fossil and non-fossil split for co-fired fuels
s: When biofuels are combusted jointly with fossil fuels, the fossil and non-fossil fractions must be separated and emission factors applied to the matching fractions.

n: Abandoned surface mine and uncontrolled combustion reporting boundary
s: CO2 from uncontrolled combustion of coal must be reported under 1.B.1.b, not under abandoned surface mines, to avoid double counting.

n: Abandoned well emission factor plugged versus unplugged split rule
s: The source says the plugged/unplugged split of abandoned well EFs requires plugging counts, and the all-wells default applies when plugging data are insufficient.

n: Biogenic CO2 reporting for charcoal and biochar

n: CO2 from COG flaring zero when all COG is recovered for energy (Tier 1b)
s: If non-fugitive coke emissions use Tier 1b, CO2 from COG flaring is taken as zero to avoid double counting.

n: CO2 projects separation rule for oil and gas fugitive emissions
s: For oil and gas projects involving CO2 injection, capture/transport/injection/storage is separated from oil and gas production, with CO2 sequestration and CO2-system fugitives assessed under Chapter 5.

n: Completeness when only a subset uses Tier 2 or Tier 3
s: When Tier 2 or Tier 3 covers only some emissions such as flaring, remaining emissions must still be accounted for.

n: Consistency of emission factors and activity data
s: Emission factors and activity data must share the same basis so that they can be combined correctly.

n: Correction of production data for net trade
s: Production data used for fugitive emission estimates should be adjusted for net imports or exports where applicable.

n: Default sour gas fraction for gas processing
s: If no sour gas fraction data are available and other options fail, a default of 32 percent sour gas may be applied in gas processing.

n: Default uncertainty for gasification transformation emission factors (Table 4.3.12)
s: Assigns an overall default uncertainty of -90% to +900% (one-tenth to ten times the mean) to CO2, CH4 and N2O emission factors for gasification transformation processes, based on expert judgement.

n: Double counting in alternative Tier 2 mass balance
s: When the alternative Tier 2 mass balance is applied, reported venting or flaring data for the same sources must not also be counted.

n: Drained methane accounting rule for Tiers 1 and 2
s: For Tier 1 and Tier 2, utilised or flared drained methane is subtracted from the total methane estimate, while drained methane vented to the atmosphere is not recounted.

n: Emission factor basis must match activity data
s: Selected emission factors must be valid for the application and expressed on the same basis as the activity data.

n: Exploration emission factor boundary for oil wells

n: Ecoregion protection and environmental flow enforcement by 2030
s: Scenario assumes protection levels for each ecoregion and environmental flow protections are introduced and enforced by 2030.

loc.section: Additional conservation policies are implemented, as required, to ensure scientifically recommended levels of protection for each ecoregion are introduced and enforced by 2030 (see Annex 7.3.2). This is modelled by preventing loss of native vegetation in areas identified as key biodiversity areas (BirdLife International 2017) or wilderness (Watson et al. 2016), and providing any additional incentives required for land use change providing biodiversity benefits (Leclere et al. 2018). The package also supports higher agricultural productivity, particularly in low- and medium- income nations (which converge towards productivity levels in high-income nations), reduced agricultural waste and food system losses, reduced barriers to agricultural trade and lower meat consumption where this promotes healthier diets. Improvements in water use efficiency are harnessed and environmental flow protections are fully enforced by 2030 (Pastor et al. 2019), reducing total agricultural water use in catchments that are currently water stressed, and ensuring all irrigated production is consistent with maintaining environmental flows and watering requirements. This combination of measures reduces near-term biodiversity loss by around a third compared to historical levels, and improves biodiversity relative to Historical Trends by the end of the century (Leclere et al. 2020).
